articles.title: Debate in New York City over city-run groceries is not just about food, but something bigger
articles.author: Nevin Cohen, Chair of the Department of Health Policy and Management, CUNY Graduate School of Public Health and Public Policy
paras: New York City is moving closer to launching its effort to counter food inflation by opening five city-run grocery stores. Mayor Zohran Mamdani announced in May 2026 that the first store would open in the Hunts Point neighborhood of the South Bronx in 2027, with another in East Harlem to follow.

Five stores, one in each borough, are unlikely to substantially change grocery prices in a city with nearly 1,000 supermarkets and more than 8 million inhabitants. But each could make a meaningful difference to the grocery bills of local shoppers by selling essentials at below-market prices.

Even with just five planned stores set to open in lower-income neighborhoods, the initiative has ignited fierce opposition from independent grocers, supermarket trade associations and a coalition representing immigrant-owned food businesses.
What explains this pushback?

As a food policy scholar, I believe this opposition is about more than the immediate economic impact of five stores. It is about the precedent they could establish. Mamdani’s initiative challenges an entrenched expectation that the government should leave the provision of consumer goods to private enterprise even as it encourages businesses to invest in certain locations, regulates their activities and helps low-income shoppers through various food assistance programs.

The reality is more complicated. For at least a century, New York’s food economy has not operated independently of government. In fact, public policies and investments have long shaped where supermarkets open, which businesses can operate with a profit, and how residents obtain food.
It’s just that they have done so in ways consumers often don’t see.

That is why the five grocery stores carry a broader significance, in my view. They offer a different model of public investment that makes the government much more visible in providing an essential service – and more accountable for its results. New Yorkers will get an opportunity to judge that contribution directly.
If the stores succeed, they may change not just what people expect to pay for groceries, but what they expect their city government to provide.
New York City has committed US$70 million to develop these stores, which will be open to all.
While they will be managed by private operators, the city will provide rent-free space, prioritize publicly owned sites and ensure that essential foods are priced 30% below typical retail prices.
In this respect, the stores offer a “public option” – a government-provided good or service that exists alongside private alternatives, like public schools and city hospitals.

Municipal grocery stores would offer New Yorkers a similar choice alongside private retailers. But as a public option, they would create a visible alternative against which shoppers can judge privately owned stores, setting a benchmark for food prices and service quality. They would also demonstrate how public investment can be used to make an essential good more affordable.
At his May announcement, Mamdani described the proposed Bronx store and its surrounding development as “physical proof of our conviction that government can be a force for good.”
A fresh form of intervention
Government-supported food retailing has a long history in New York City despite opposition by existing businesses.

In 1934, Mayor Fiorello La Guardia’s administration began selling discounted milk to low-income families, but the initiative drew complaints from grocers about unfair competition. Independent merchants similarly protested the city’s efforts to subsidize a new Pathmark supermarket in East Harlem in the 1990s, warning that it would put local grocers out of business.

A more recent example is the city’s Food Retail Expansion to Support Health program, known as FRESH. Since 2009, it has offered supermarket developers and operators long-term tax breaks and zoning incentives to build or expand dozens of stores in underserved neighborhoods.
These incentives have helped increase grocery retail space, but shoppers don’t see the public support behind them.

FRESH is just one example of an approach toward supermarket financing that gained momentum in the 1990s, when governments sought to address social problems by encouraging private investment. Food insecurity was blamed on a scarcity of neighborhood supermarkets, not on prices being beyond reach for local shoppers.

Subsidizing new stores promised better nutrition and economic development without confronting poverty or inequality, and FRESH reflects that approach. Participating supermarkets must devote space to perishable foods, but they’re not required to offer affordable prices. That may be one reason why researchers have found that adding supermarkets to low-income neighborhoods, by itself, doesn’t substantially improve residents’ diets.

This hidden government role is hardly confined to grocery stores. Much of what government does for Americans is delivered indirectly, through tax credits, subsidies and private institutions. Because the public contribution is obscured, people often give credit to private markets for the benefits provided by public policy, from student loans to healthcare.
This invisibility is a consequence of policy design and influences how citizens understand government, a phenomenon that political scientist Suzanne Mettler described as “the submerged state.”
Bringing the state into the open
Municipal grocery stores depart from the traditional model in two important ways.

First, they make affordability an explicit condition of public investment rather than the outcome of increased retail competition. Second, they make government’s contribution visible. For example, the stores will share distinct branding so shoppers know who’s responsible for the affordable food.

If the stores deliver reliable savings, shoppers may begin to see affordable food as something government can help provide, not an outcome determined entirely by private markets. When public benefits are obscured, people are more likely to underestimate government’s contribution to their lives. Visible programs, like a physical store in the neighborhood, make that contribution easier to notice and evaluate.

Visibility also creates accountability. A customer at a private supermarket that received a tax break to expand isn’t likely to tie the store’s prices or food quality to government policy. At a municipal grocery store, with clear branding, the connection is unmistakable.

To be sure, critics’ concerns deserve serious attention. Many independent grocery stores are owned by immigrant entrepreneurs operating on thin margins. Groups representing bodegas and independent supermarkets warn that a publicly subsidized competitor could draw away their customers. Some may lose business.

Yet East Harlem’s Pathmark demonstrates that new supermarkets and smaller retailers can coexist. Between 2000 and 2015, the number of small grocery stores and bodegas in the neighborhood increased from 100 to 126, while supermarkets rose from 10 to 18. That said, those figures don’t establish Pathmark’s effects on individual businesses.

The municipal stores’ impact on nearby retailers remains an open question. But the task for New York City is to ensure that private operators deliver excellent service and real savings, and that their commercial interests don’t undermine the public mission. It will also need to provide good working conditions and track effects on nearby businesses.
Ultimately, public ownership doesn’t guarantee success. But it makes government’s responsibility for the outcome impossible to miss.
Nevin Cohen receives research funding from the City of New York.

articles.title: Republican gerrymandering worked pretty well in Texas and Florida, even if it backfired in North Carolina and Ohio
articles.author: Charlie Hunt, Associate Professor of Political Science, Boise State University
paras: During the 2026 election cycle, Republicans enacted a series of gerrymanders – a form of partisan redistricting – in a handful of states to give them a disproportionate edge over Democrats in their congressional delegations. Democrats responded with a successful redistricting effort in California and an unsuccessful one in Virginia.
Gerrymandering has obvious implications for fairness and democracy, characterized by some as politicians picking their voters, not voters picking their politicians.
There’s also a practical consideration for those doing the gerrymandering: The efforts can fail when they overplay their hand.

By spreading their supportive voters across many districts, parties can create more seats that may lean in their direction. But if spread too thin, these efforts can backfire and net seats for the other party, particularly in a “wave” election year that favors the other party. This unintended consequence is often referred to as a “dummymander.”
So, with such massive Democratic majorities poised to enter the 120th Congress, did Republican attempts to gerrymander actually end up costing them some seats in the U.S. House?
The answer isn’t as clear-cut as you might think.
Dummymanders in North Carolina and Ohio?

Republican state legislatures in Ohio and North Carolina redrew their congressional maps in 2025, crafting a set of districts they believed would maximize the number of seats they could win in the House.

Despite both states being traditionally competitive in statewide elections, their state legislatures drew a collection of seats Republicans believed they would win: 12 of these 15 new seats in Ohio and 11 out of 14 in North Carolina included a majority of voters who voted for Donald Trump in the 2024 presidential election.

But in 2026, Democrats across the country won dozens of seats that had previously seemed out of reach, including districts Trump won by double digits in 2024. Many of these seats were in heavily gerrymandered Republican seats.

In Ohio and North Carolina, the size and scope of the midterm backlash against Trump and his party put many of the seats Republicans targeted in these states, including ones Trump won by as many as 20 points, in serious jeopardy.
In the end, the Democratic wave overcame so many Trump-won seats in these states that their new delegations to Congress may be more Democratic than they would have been without the gerrymanders.
Democrats held the line in the deep South

Texas and Florida also targeted a series of Democrat-held seats to flip their way in 2026. Nine such seats across these two states, as well as a vulnerable seat held by Democratic U.S. Rep. Shomari Figures in Alabama, were the targets of gerrymanders that created new districts that Trump won in 2024, all by 9 percentage points or more.

But once the 2026 Democratic wave swept through the deep South, these gerrymanders were essentially canceled out. Despite the gains the party projected, Republicans in these three states appear likely to enter the 120th Congress with delegations the same size as they had in the 119th.

Other Republican gerrymandering attempts were successful, but only barely. In Tennessee’s 9th District, the last remaining Democratic seat in the state was gerrymandered into a district Donald Trump won by 21 points in 2024. Republicans did hold that seat as expected, but only by 2,500 votes, or just over 1 percentage point.
Gerrymanders that worked – and didn’t
Many of these gerrymanders were not maximally successful. But were they true dummymanders?
In North Carolina and Ohio it does appear that Republicans overplayed their hand by counting on past Trump voters in a national environment that proved so favorable to the Democrats.

In Ohio, a gerrymander that aimed for a two-thirds Republican majority in their House delegation will net them less than half of that in the 120th Congress. That outcome ended up producing a more representative result, one that was roughly in line with the two parties’ 2026 popular vote shares in the state.

North Carolina was a more drastic dummymander: The Republicans aimed to design districts where they would win seats accounting for almost two-thirds of their congressional delegation. But the party is currently poised to hold, at best, less than one-third of their state’s seats.

And California, which Democrats gerrymandered in reaction to Republican efforts in other states, is a partisan success story. The state is projected to send only 8% of their delegation to the House as Republicans, despite voting 30% for Republicans statewide.

In Texas and Florida the story is more complicated. Democrats in those states retained most of the seats they held that their Republican legislatures targeted in their gerrymanders, thanks to historic shifts by Hispanic voters who had voted for Trump in the 2024 election.

But gerrymanders can be effective beyond marginal, targeted districts. Taken as a whole, Texas’ and Florida’s district boundaries were drawn so favorably for Republicans that even a Democratic tsunami managed only to keep these states’ delegations identical in the next Congress, since many other districts remained safe for Republicans.

In these states, Republicans still enjoy a greater proportion of House seats than their popular vote margins would reflect. And in a less Democrat-leaning election cycle, many of these gerrymandered seats could very well shift back toward Republicans.
Failed GOP gerrymanders would have produced an even bigger blue wave

As poor as the outcome of the 2026 midterms was for Republicans, it could have been even worse. In fact, some Republican states might count themselves lucky that their attempts to gerrymander failed in the lead-up to the midterms.

In traditionally Republican states such as Missouri and Utah, courts struck down gerrymanders that would have created a series of districts that Trump won by around 20 percentage points. If the gerrymanders had not been struck down, Democrats’ shocking success in similar districts across the country could have netted them as many as five additional seats in these states.

A similar situation played out in Indiana and South Carolina. New maps pushed by Trump that failed in their state legislatures were intended to produce even more lopsided Republican gains. But analysis from the Cook Political Report found that these maps might have netted Democrats as many as six out of South Carolina’s seven House seats, and eight out of Indiana’s nine. Instead, Democrats seem likely to end up with only a pair of seats in each state.
What’s next in gerrymandering wars?
The 2026 election cycle demonstrates that gerrymandering is a far more complex and dynamic proposition than it is often treated by pundits and parties.

Wave elections of this size can often overcome the intended effects of gerrymandered maps, but subsequent elections might find them much more effective. Plus, parties often draw gerrymandered maps based on the previous election’s presidential results – a measure that may be less reliable as voters continue to make more unexpected choices.

Moreover, both red and blue states are dealing with the aftermath of the Louisiana v. Callais Supreme Court decision, which made the gerrymandering of racial groups easier to do without court interventions. Over the next two years, Republicans may attempt to implement even more new maps in many new states, particularly in the South. Those new districts will likely aim to dilute majority-Black districts that are no longer protected by the Voting Rights Act.
Meanwhile, Democratic state governments appear poised to continue with their pushback against last cycle’s Republican efforts with gerrymanders of their own over the next two years.
But the Republican redistricting failures of the 2026 cycle, including their near misses, should make both parties cautious about future attempts.

articles.title: Allegheny County has more license plate readers than any other Pa. county. Here’s what’s at stake
articles.author: TK Vinod Kumar, Faculty in the Law, Criminal Justice and Society Program., University of Pittsburgh
paras: Surveillance is a reality in the modern world. Security cameras record streets, stores, home entrances and even highways – and our phones keep track of where we go. Most of us likely don’t want to live like the characters in George Orwell’s novel “1984,” where an all-seeing government, Big Brother, is always watching. Yet technology used to fight crime has greatly increased the level of surveillance around the world.
In the United States, one technology in particular has become a focus of that debate: automated license plate readers.

These cameras, often mounted on poles at intersections and highway ramps, photograph every passing car. They record its plate, make, color and location, then store that information in searchable databases that police can check against lists of wanted vehicles. Flock Safety, one of the largest vendors, has cameras in thousands of U.S. communities, and their spread has prompted growing concern about privacy.
Allegheny County in southwestern Pennsylvania, home to Pittsburgh, has 827 automated license plate readers, more than any other county in the state.

Critics warn that the cameras can map people’s daily lives with little oversight, while police say they help find stolen cars and missing people. In the borough of Munhall, just outside of Pittsburgh, residents petitioned to remove two Flock cameras on Main Street.

Pennsylvania lawmakers from both parties have proposed at least nine bills, ranging from an outright ban of these devices to warrant requirements. In October the state House passed a bill that would limit their use and how long data is kept.

I study policing and public order in democracies, and I spent more than 30 years in police administration in India and with United Nations missions abroad. I’ve seen firsthand how new technologies can help police and why they need guardrails.

How extensively police use surveillance technologies can fall anywhere across a spectrum. At one end, cameras can be positioned to monitor virtually every vehicle and person within a specified area. At the other, they are deployed sparingly and aimed only at specific vehicles or people, such as stolen cars or past offenders.

Mass surveillance may entail systemic collection of data of large numbers of people in the public space, including those not suspected of any violations. These can include networks of license plate readers that capture all vehicle traveling through an area, or cameras using facial recognition to analyze images of individuals in public spaces against existing databases.

Targeted uses include matching the vehicle numbers or faces of people of interest. These could be past offenders or people whose behavior raises suspicion, such as someone lingering near a bank late at night. Another example is designating certain places, such as airports, military bases, courthouses or power plants, as high-security areas and deploying surveillance technology there, with or without informing the public.

In the middle could be the sweet spot: calibrated use of such technology at an optimum level agreed on through laws or regulations. The level could be measured by the number of cameras in a city, the density of devices per square mile or even the terabytes of data collected.
Risks of mass surveillance

Mass surveillance carries the inherent risk of the state collecting extensive information on its entire population, or on large segments of it, which creates significant potential for misuse. The state could guarantee that the data would be handled responsibly. Even so, the data could be misused on purpose, or accessed by unauthorized persons because of vulnerabilities in data security.

There is also the fear of “surveillance creep.” That is when technologies adopted for one purpose expand into others. License plate readers, for example, are typically sold to communities as a way to find stolen cars, missing children and suspects in serious crimes. But police have also used them to monitor protests. According to records obtained by nonprofit advocacy group the Electronic Frontier Foundation, agencies across the country searched Flock’s network hundreds of times in connection with protests over a single year.

The potential benefits of surveillance for crime prevention appear to be significant. A 2026 study of 216 law enforcement agencies found that after they installed fixed plate-reader networks, car thefts fell relative to other property crimes, and more theft cases were solved by arrest. In Atlantic City, New Jersey, a major expansion of plate readers didn’t reduce violent crime overall, but it was associated with fewer shootings, car thefts and property crimes.
Other law enforcement areas that could benefit from the technology include drug running and human trafficking.

In Pittsburgh, plate-reader data feeds into the police bureau’s real-time crime center. The data collected could be matched in real time with law enforcement and other databases to track the movement of offenders.
That could be used to prevent a wide range of crimes, from thefts and robberies to drug running and human trafficking, or to help solve cold cases.

Limited use of such technology has the benefit of curbing misuse while still using it in a controlled manner against known offenders and threats. That means using it on a person-to-person basis with prior legal or judicial approval or in high-security areas.
In this context, it would be most appropriate to take three steps to address law enforcement data collection generally:

Keep requiring police to get court warrants backed by probable cause for cellphone location data – records showing which cell towers a phone has connected to. That includes closing the loophole that lets agencies buy the same data from commercial brokers without a warrant.
Put in place federal or state laws restricting the use of facial recognition, with suitable judicial oversight.
Have county and municipal agencies regulate the use of surveillance cameras in public areas.

Pennsylvania’s proposals span this range and beyond. State Sen. Dan Laughlin, an Erie Republican, would ban the cameras outright. U.S. Rep. Pat Harrigan proposes legislation requiring police to get a warrant before searching plate-reader data. And the bill the state House passed in October sits in the middle, allowing the cameras but limiting their uses and how long data is kept.

Decisions regarding the use of mass cameras should not be left to law enforcement agencies. They are interested in crime control, which could color their judgment. Those decisions are best left to elected representatives at the federal, state and local levels, with input from legal experts and relevant law enforcement agencies.

In my view, mandatory public consultation before deploying such systems in a community would improve the legitimacy of the program and of the implementing government. Regular audits are a common safeguard when government agencies use intrusive technology. Pennsylvania’s House-passed plate-reader bill, for instance, would require agencies to adopt audit policies. Such audits could happen as often as twice a year, with information and analyses available to the community or to affected individuals on request.

Transparency of the process would go a long way toward enhancing public trust. The opposite can erode it. At Penn State, for example, the university initially declined to say how many plate-reader cameras it had installed or where, drawing criticism from students before it ended its contract with Flock.

Another precaution is to keep the data from being available in raw form to nongovernmental entities, especially corporations. Location records can be valuable to businesses. Companies already use plate-reader data for purposes such as verifying a loan applicant’s home address.
As Pennsylvania lawmakers weigh new limits, the choices they make may help determine how close any of us come to living in an Orwellian state.

articles.title: Cathy Come Home at 60: many of the housing issues the film exposed still exist today
articles.author: Jessica Field, Research Associate,  Humanitarian and Conflict Response Institute, University of Manchester
paras: “You don’t care. You only pretend to care!” an exhausted, homeless Cathy shouts at a board of welfare officials just days before her children are taken from her. It’s a scene from Cathy Come Home, the 1966 BBC drama that remains – 60 years on – a touchstone for discussions on homelessness.

Written by Jeremy Sandford and directed by Ken Loach, the television play follows Cathy and her husband Reg, who are expecting a child when Reg loses his income through injury. The couple then lose their home, the first of many instances of this. Eventually Cathy ends up, with three children in tow, at an overcrowded government hostel that doesn’t permit husbands. Cathy finally loses her children to the care system, leaving her broken and alone on a railway platform.

Despite its age, the film is recognised even by people who were not yet born when it was first screened. As recently as 2016, it spawned a new initiative: Homes for Cathy, a network of housing associations and charities kickstarted to “end homelessness”.

Studies have highlighted controversy and debate as key to cementing the film’s cultural status. Though the main cast were actors, Loach employed groundbreaking techniques to present a composite of things that had genuinely happened to people over the preceding 18 months.

He filmed in real locations, used improvised dialogue and captured authentic encounters between the couple and gatekeepers to housing – people like landlords. A narrator also listed facts about housing poverty over the visuals. One of the most damning statistics from the time hangs as text over the closing frame: “4,000 children are separated from their parents and taken into care each year because their parents are homeless.”

For decades, media and government figures argued about the veracity of the statistics, how accurate Cathy’s experience was and whether it was right to blend fact and fiction in this way. The ordinariness of fact-based drama today (things like Mr Bates vs The Post Office from 2024) is testament to Cathy Come Home’s experimentation with the format.

The more pressing reason for its relevance is the endurance of its central theme: homelessness. Numbers of people living in temporary accommodation are unprecedented in recent times: 135,580 households in England – including 177,530 children.

Terrible conditions persist, too. Temporary accommodation is often “unfit for human habitation”, as a government housing committee recently found. This can include homes riddled with damp and mould, or with broken fixtures and fittings, or safety issues. Between 2019 and 2025, temporary accommodation was listed as a contributing factor in the deaths of 104 children.

The film’s enduring impact also rests on the belief that it changed things in British society. For months, newspapers covered their own “Cathy” stories. My recent work with the charity Justlife on temporary accommodation history shows the film wasn’t the first spotlight on these conditions; homeless families had been publicly protesting about their treatment for years. But when the BBC broadcast Cathy’s experiences to 12 million viewers, so many people called in that the switchboard was overwhelmed.

Housing campaign charity Shelter – coincidentally founded two weeks after Cathy Come Home aired – capitalised on the attention by presenting families like Cathy’s in campaign materials and involving actress Carol White in rallies. The charity had raised around £50,000 by 1967 – not all due to Cathy Come Home, but it certainly helped.

The film is also credited with the formation of homelessness charity Crisis in 1967. Politicians even spoke of the drama in parliament, and the minister of housing invited Loach, Sandford and producer Tony Garnett to meet him in Whitehall to discuss the issues it raised.

However, there was no significant change to homelessness law until the Housing (Homeless Persons) Act in 1977 – 11 years after the film. This legally defined homelessness and gave those who met priority-need criteria and were not deemed “intentionally” homeless a right to be rehoused. The law came about primarily due to civil service concerns about how councils were managing homelessness, as well as pressure from housing campaigners. Cathy Come Home was part of that wider story.

Loach and others have credited the film with ending family separation in some areas at the time. Certainly, after a series of public meetings – one of which included Loach, Sandford and homeless families – the council in Birmingham (where parts of the drama were filmed) committed to trying to end family separation within two years. Yet a 1972 Shelter report highlighted the practice continued in the city – and elsewhere. It didn’t end there: an investigation revealed that in 2022-23 at least 50 children were taken into care for the central reason of homelessness.

There were issues with the film’s representation of the period, however. It has been criticised for focusing on the experiences of white homeless people, even though Black and ethnic minority households were more likely to be homeless or living in poor-quality housing.

These concerns remain pertinent. Today, Black-led households are more likely to apply for statutory homelessness support, spend more time in temporary accommodation, and are less likely to be rehoused in social housing than their white counterparts.

Cathy’s family presented the nuclear ideal, too, when unmarried mothers or women fleeing relationship breakdown or domestic violence typically faced much higher barriers to accommodation. Similarly today, single-parent households are nearly four times more likely to be homeless than two-parent families.

Sixty years after Cathy Come Home first aired, many of the problems it depicted remain unresolved. Each anniversary offers a valuable opportunity to hold a mirror up to today and demand affordable, safe and secure housing for everyone. But to do that, we must pay attention to its silences and what it failed to achieve as much as what it depicted.
Jessica Field consulted for Justlife on the report: Lifelines: A history of temporary accommodation in England, 1834-2011.

articles.title: The 2% tax hike on rental income is bad for landlords and tenants alike. Here’s what reform looks like
articles.author: Emma Laurie, Emerita Fellow, University of Southampton
paras: The October budget brought unwelcome news for private landlords in England, Wales and Northern Ireland. From April 2027, they will pay a further 2% tax on rental income, in addition to the 2% increase announced in the 2025 budget.

Given the notoriously high cost of private renting in the UK, there may be little sympathy for landlords. And the new tax rise will most likely be passed on to tenants through rent increases anyway – a view shared by both the National Residential Landlords Association and the UK’s public finance watchdog.

I’m a law professor specialising in social and private rental markets. I believe that the new tax represents a major missed opportunity. Instead of increasing landlords’ tax burden – and indirectly raising rents for tenants – the government could have taken the chance to negotiate with landlords to cap rent increases.
But given that the new tax will probably be passed on to renters, how much power do tenants themselves have to resist rent hikes?
The Renters’ Rights Act 2025 was rightly hailed as a landmark change in tenants’ rights. It abolished the notorious section 21 “no fault” eviction, effective as of May 1, 2026.

But the act is very unlikely to protect tenants from a rent increase that is in line with the going rate. Landlords can only give notice to raise the rent once a year, and must provide a minimum of two months’ notice. Tenants can challenge an increase by applying to a tribunal, but they will only be successful if the new rent is more expensive than the local market rate.

Both tenants and landlords are encouraged to provide information about rents for other similar properties. There is no single approved source for such information, but websites such as Zoopla and Rightmove are typically used.

Before applying to the tribunal, it is sensible to try to reach agreement over the rent. The 2025 act does give tenants much greater flexibility. They can now end a tenancy with two months’ notice, whereas before the act, tenancies would often have a defined duration, for example 12 months. This means that tenants are no longer tied to paying for a tenancy that has become unaffordable. It may also make landlords more willing to negotiate to keep good tenants.
But the broader point remains: the 2025 act cannot protect against rent increases in areas where demand outstrips supply.

When the Renters’ Rights Act was going through Parliament, the government was adamant that rent caps would not be introduced. At the time, I argued that it was part of an unspoken deal to win landlords’ support for abolishing section 21 evictions.
How the government can protect renters

Rent controls are a source of controversy in the UK, largely because of the legacy of measures in force for most of the 20th century. But since rents were brought out of control by Margaret Thatcher’s government in 1988, the private rental sector has adopted a classically neoliberal approach.

There is no universally agreed definition of neoliberalism. In housing, it generally means that private landlords should be free to charge market rents for homes that offer relatively little stability.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has recently recognised that the neoliberal model “simply doesn’t work well enough for ordinary people”. What, then, is the alternative?

Instead of imposing the additional 2% tax on landlords, the government could have taken a first step to making renting more affordable by getting landlord support to cap rent increases. In other words, a trade-off between tax income, benefiting the government, and rent capping, which would potentially benefit tenants.
Rent control measures have become increasingly sophisticated, but they are certainly not a silver bullet for the housing crisis.

However, reducing landlords’ tax obligations in exchange for modest price capping – for example by tying rises to the Consumer Prices Index, as Scotland has done – could work for landlords and renters alike.

Landlords have long expressed dissatisfaction with the numerous changes to their tax position since 2015. They do have a point: cumulative changes have made the English tax and regulation regime one of the least favourable in Europe and North America.

Any such deal would, of course, mean the government giving up the expected additional tax income – estimated at £35 million in 2027-28 and £445 million by 2030-31. But if the prime minister is serious about moving away from a rental housing market dominated by four decades of neoliberal thinking, this proposal would represent a modest first step in the right direction – one that would benefit everyone.

articles.title: While California’s wealth tax failed, states are taking other steps to collect more revenue from the rich
articles.author: Allison Anna Tait, Professor of Law, University of Richmond
paras: State efforts to tax the rich did relatively well in the 2026 midterm elections, following a series of state legislative moves in that direction in recent years.

That might come as a surprise because a majority of voters rejected California’s Proposition 40. The much-publicized ballot initiative would have imposed a one-time 5% tax on the net worth of the state’s roughly 200 billionaires. Google co-founder Sergey Brin and several other billionaires spent nearly $400 million trying to persuade voters to reject it.
Emmanuel Saez, a University of California, Berkeley economist who studies inequality and helped design Proposition 40, lamented the loss, saying: “Today oligarchy has won.”

As a law professor who recently wrote a book about wealth inequality, I have been monitoring the results of these efforts aimed at taxing the rich. Despite Proposition 40’s failure, I think it’s important to observe that many Americans expressed support during the midterms for hiking income taxes on the rich, and to a lesser extent, taxes on the second – or third or fourth – homes the very wealthy possess.
Taxing the rich at the ballot box
Taxing income is proving a more successful strategy than taxing wealth.

Major changes to income taxes were up for a vote in five states during the midterms. Three of those ballot initiatives were proposals that sought to boost income tax rates on the rich or maintain those rates. All three prevailed.

In Washington state, for example, voters backed a measure that will preserve its new 9.9% income tax on household income above $1 million. This “millionaire’s tax,” signed into law earlier in 2026, is the state’s first personal income tax.

Meanwhile, Colorado voters rejected Proposition 136, which would have capped the state’s income tax rate at 4.4%. They also approved Amendment 87, a new graduated income tax that raises rates on households and businesses with incomes over $500,000.

And even though California’s voters rejected Proposition 40, they did approve Proposition 3. That measure makes permanent the income tax rates enacted in 2012 for the state’s highest earners, which were set to expire in 2031. The surcharges, adjusted annually for inflation, start at 10.3% for incomes of $360,000 and go up to a 12.3% surcharge for taxpayers earning over $721,000.

And in August 2026, Missouri voters overwhelmingly rejected a measure that would have required the state’s lawmakers to eliminate its income tax. This would have meant losing $8.5 billion in revenue annually. The change would have let rich income taxpayers off the hook and replaced lost revenue through an increased sales tax that would have hit low-income taxpayers hardest.

The two losses were in North Carolina and Iowa. Neither state voted directly on a tax to be levied on the rich. But both approved constitutional amendments that will make it harder for the state legislatures to enact these kinds of taxes in the future. North Carolina’s governor, Josh Stein, called the amendment in his state a “millionaire protection cap.”
State legislatures raising income tax rates on high earners
Ahead of the midterms, new taxes on the rich introduced via state legislatures, rather than ballot initiatives, also emerged.

In Maine, legislators voted in April 2026 for a tax surcharge of 1% on income over $1 million. The following month, Hawaiian lawmakers created a new 13% income bracket for single taxpayers earning above $500,000 or couples filing jointly who make over $1 million. This change is paired with a reduction in rates for lower-income brackets.
And one month after that, Rhode Island enacted a surcharge for millionaires’ income to be phased in over the next three years, reaching a maximum 3% rate.

In 2009, New York became one of the first states to pass one of these high-earner income taxes. Washington, D.C., Massachusetts and Maryland also enacted these “millionaire taxes” in 2022, 2023 and 2025, respectively.

Another way that state and local governments are boosting the tax revenue they get from wealthy constituents is by levying special taxes on pricey homes that aren’t the owners’ primary residences. These initiatives have succeeded both in state legislatures and voting booths.

Montana lawmakers, in April 2025, approved a new tiered property tax system, which took effect on Jan. 1, 2026. It raised property tax rates on vacation homes and short-term rentals to 1.9%, while primary residences and qualifying long-term rentals pay lower, tiered homestead rates.

New York City rolled out its “pied-à-terre tax” in July. The new tax imposes an annual surcharge of 0.8% to 1.3% on single-family homes valued at $5 million or more, and 4% to 6.5% on condos and co-ops valued at $1 million or more. The surcharge only applies to homes that are not a primary residence.

Rhode Island has a similar property tax that took effect at the same time as New York City’s. It’s an annual surcharge of $2.50 for every $500 of assessed value above $1 million that applies to non-primary residences.

And on Nov. 3, voters in Boulder, Colorado, approved a residential vacancy tax on homes that sit empty more than half the year. The surcharge, which goes into effect in 2028, will be roughly $4,000 a year for each vacant property. It applies across the board, but homes that aren’t primary residences are the clear target.
However, just west of Boulder in Crested Butte, Colorado, a second-home tax failed. So did an effort to levy a similar surcharge in San Diego, California.
Why income taxes are attractive to voters and lawmakers
There is a good reason why taxing the income of rich people is easier to pull off than taxing their wealth: Income taxes are much easier to calculate.

Income taxes can be based on annual income tax filings, whether state or federal. It requires no extra work to value someone’s net worth. There are no such filings for wealth, except after death, if a large estate is left behind.
Wealth taxes also require the annual valuation of businesses, farmland, artwork, intellectual property and other assets – many of which are hard to estimate.

The downside of taxing income instead of wealth is that it limits how much revenue can be raised from the people most able to pay taxes. Most wealthy people convert little of their wealth into income. One common exception occurs when they sell some of their stock.
Property taxes, like income taxes, are an exception to this rule. Calculating how much tax on real estate someone owes is easy for the authorities to do using annual municipal assessments.
Despite Proposition 40’s defeat, it looks like Americans are generally open to taxing wealthy people more – at least when the states do it.
In Illinois, where a billionaire governor, JB Pritzer, easily won a third term, another interesting ballot initiative prevailed.

More than 75% of voters in Cook County, which includes Chicago and several of its suburbs, approved a nonbinding, advisory referendum asking if Illinois should adopt the “millionaire amendment for property tax relief and education.” It would levy a new surcharge of 3% on incomes over $1 million. While this win did not authorize a new tax, it revealed that support for one would be strong – at least in Chicago and Evanston.
Even billionaire Bill Gates has said he believes a “billionaire’s tax” will be necessary. The question is: What kind?

articles.title: Slapps, NDAs and gendered ‘lawfare’: how the rich and powerful silence victims of sexual offences
articles.author: Francesca Farrington, Lecturer in Law,  School of Law and Social Justice, University of Liverpool
paras: The conviction of Russell Brand came nearly two decades after “Me Too” was coined. Yet the years the former comedian avoided accountability serve as a stark reminder of the dangers victims still face when speaking out. The truth is that women who name predators are increasingly at risk of legal proceedings.

While the #MeToo movement emboldened victims to speak truth to power, it also exposed the tactics offenders use to silence them. UN special rapporteur Irene Khan, described this as a “perverse twist” in the age of #MeToo.

Research has shed light on what’s really happening here – mechanisms designed to provide justice can be used to suppress victims and provide impunity for those with money and power. So how can this happen in countries that are supposed to be committed to fundamental rights and the rule of law?

Across the world, powerful people are evading scrutiny by threatening legal action that could leave their accusers ruined financially. When powerful people use the law, or even just the threat of it, to suppress criticism, it is known as strategic lawsuits against public participation (Slapp).

You might wonder why courts don’t simply dismiss these cases. In practice, it is rare that they even make it before a judge, because the threat is often enough to push a settlement. For many, as one victim said, “silence is the only way to survive”. The aim is not to win the case, but to turn the process of defending the action into a punishment.

Slapps take many forms. Many people might picture a corporation or politician suing a public watchdog. Less well known are Slapps targeting victims of sexual and gender-based violence (SGBV). Often referred to as a kind of gendered censorship or gendered lawfare, these lawsuits are prevalent and equally chilling. Rather than seeking justice, these legal tactics are used to create fear, financial pressure and a culture of self-censorship.

When reporting on SGBV, the stakes are high enough for large media organisations. So imagine how high they are for victims. In 2023, a woman called Nina Cresswell shared her story of sexual abuse on social media. It related to an incident in 2010, and Cresswell said she was motivated to speak out by guilt at the thought of another woman suffering what she had gone through.

But just days later, her alleged abuser sued her for defamation. The lawsuit did three things. By suing Cresswell, the perpetrator denied the abuse, attacked his accuser, and recast himself as the victim. This tactic is known as Darvo – Deny, Attack, Reverse Victim and Offender. It has become an integral part of gendered-Slapp suits. Cresswell won her case, but she lost almost three years of her life to litigation. No police action was taken against the man.

Brand has been accused of similar tactics. He reportedly obtained an anti-harassment injunction against Szilvia Berki after she made allegations against him. The injunction – which is still in place – is far-reaching and prohibits Berki from repeating her allegations, including to friends and family.

She was left with £50,000 in legal costs, and the judge authorised Brand’s lawyers to begin bankruptcy proceedings against her. While the full story behind the injunction appears to be complicated, Berki’s experience shows the scope of these gagging orders and the financial cost associated with fighting one.

Entertainer David Walliams attempted to secure an injunction to suppress claims of sexual misconduct. While he denies all allegations against him, his application was refused and the findings of investigations by The Guardian and ITV News are now public.

Non-disclosure agreements (NDAs) are also a major part of gendered censorship. For years, contracts were used to silence victims and witnesses of SGBV. Zelda Perkins, a former personal assistant to disgraced US film producer Harvey Weinstein, was bound by an NDA after she tried to expose his predatory behaviour.

In a remarkable act of courage, she broke her NDA, exposing herself to substantial legal risk. She has been campaigning for reform ever since. On an episode of the News Agents podcast, Perkins revealed that she believes there are several women who entered into NDAs with Brand.
Ending gendered censorship

There is no silver bullet in this struggle, yet there has been some progress. In the UK, the Victims and Courts Act 2026 voids any provision in an agreement that prevents a disclosure relating to criminal conduct. And the Employment Rights Act 2025 protects a worker’s right to disclose harassment and discrimination.

But more must be done. Perkins warned that Slapps – “the evil cousin of NDAs”, remain a real threat to victims. When it comes to combatting them, the UK lags behind other countries. In the UK, Slapp targets are only protected when reporting on economic and financial crime, and even then, only to a limited extent. Victims of SGBV are left largely unprotected.

Parliament is debating whether to extend protections to everyone speaking out on public interest matters. But recent reports have been a reminder that stronger anti-Slapp protections are needed to prevent the law becoming an instrument of the powerful against those alleging abuse.

Francesca Farrington has consulted on SLAPPs for the United Nations, the European Parliament, and the Coalition Against SLAPPs in Europe. She also acts as a TrialWatch expert for the Clooney Foundation for Justice.

articles.title: How groomers operate – and why victims become trapped
articles.author: Emily Chiang, Research Associate, Aston Institute for Forensic Linguistics, Aston University
paras: Entertainer and children’s author David Walliams is alleged to have used his fame to approach teenage girls, in some cases reportedly initiating sexual contact with them. Walliams has denied the allegations, but the claims raise some familiar tropes about grooming: why did she go, why didn’t she say no, why didn’t she tell anyone?
After a legal battle, ITV News and The Guardian have now published the findings of a three-year investigation into Walliams, reporting allegations that date back to 2003.

In this and other cases, there will always be people who focus not on the claims, but on the young person and what they should have done differently. Linguistic research on how grooming actually works suggests that this instinct is exactly the result that grooming is designed to produce.

Many people imagine sexual grooming as a recognisable and clearly staged process. Build friendship, then trust, then secrecy – all leading towards the offender’s ultimate goal of sexual gratification. But if this were the case, victims could notice the steps and walk away.

Along with a colleague, I undertook linguistic analysis of real chatroom conversations between convicted offenders and adult volunteers posing as 12 to 14-year-old girls. The conversations were made public by the now defunct organisation Perverted Justice, whose activity led to the apprehension and conviction of the offenders. In our analysis, we did not find the pattern mentioned above.

We identified 14 recurring “moves” – parts of the offenders’ language that have particular functions. These include building rapport (for instance by sharing personal stories), assessing risk by checking parents’ schedules or the presence of a boyfriend, escalating sexual topics and planning offline meetings. But these moves overlapped and repeated, with no typical structure emerging.
Rather, offenders seemed to tailor their grooming styles, perhaps according to their individual goals and who they believed they were talking to.

What was consistent was the large amount of rapport-building, which often ran through the whole interaction. Grooming research invariably shows that rapport-building and trust development are the central devices used to persuade and manipulate.

This may be through compliments, sharing personal information and declarations of trust. Grooming strategies are designed to develop intimacy and trust, isolate the victim and dismantle the “red flags” that might alert them to the manipulative nature of the conversation. Trust development makes it much harder for victims to notice devious intentions – there is no obvious point at which the young person has failed to spot something plainly visible.

Offenders in our data spent much of their conversations sizing up their targets. They would try to work out whether a target was likely to engage, suited their preferences, was accessible and unlikely to expose them. We called this a “risk-reward ratio assessment” – in other words, a judgement about whether this person was worth their effort.

In another study, we examined the case of an offender who took a scattergun approach, in this case targeting nearly 1,000 potential young victims. This individual would strategically cycle through an array of fake online personas to identify the one most likely to “hook” his target. The vast majority ignored or rejected his first advance, at which point they were dropped. But this is the point of the scattergun approach; a small percentage, usually the most vulnerable, will respond.
Our work also revealed how offenders manage the risk of being caught. For many we studied, a key strategy was to use language that shifted responsibility on to the target.

Questions were often formulated to elicit sexually explicit content by positioning the target as the one in control. The groomer might say, for example, “how far do you want to go”, “tell me what you wanna do”. This phrasing both presumes interest and makes declining more difficult, while laying the groundwork to say later that the young person had led the conversation.

Another feature was what we termed the “mitigating lol”. This could be something like “u should send me a nude vid lol”. This served to reduce the impact of a sexual question by implying playfulness. It also supports future claims that the requests was insincere – possibly a useful tactic in a trial. We can only infer the purpose, but it points to the same strategy of building in deniability.

I cannot speak directly to the Walliams allegations, but when it comes to celebrities in general, the task of building trust and rapport may well be easier. The victims already feel they know them, and are made to feel special by being approached. It’s also easy to see how the perks of celebrity could do much of the persuasive work.

A widely used definition of grooming across linguistics and psychology describes preparing the child, their significant adults and the wider environment for abuse. Compliance and secrecy are explicit goals. They are not evidence of the victim’s character.

So when people ask, “why did they keep replying?” or “why did they go to the house?” they are asking why a technique that was designed to engage did in fact keep them engaged. When we ask, “why didn’t they tell anyone?” we are questioning why a strategy engineered to cultivate silence did exactly that.

Grooming involves a complex network of strategies. But we know it is never the young person’s behaviour that’s the problem. The “perfect victim” who resists every advance and raises the alarm at every opportunity is a myth.

Better understanding of the strategies can help caregivers, educators and children to recognise grooming earlier. It should also shape what we say to victims after the fact. Let’s stop asking why they gave their email address, why they went to the house, why they didn’t tell anyone. Let’s question instead the actions of those responsible.

articles.title: The uncomfortable question at the heart of Europe’s identity crisis
articles.author: Kristoffer Bayer, PhD candidate, Department of Philosophy and History of Ideas, Aarhus University
paras: What makes someone French, German, British or Danish? Is it the passport they hold, the language they speak, or the ancestry they inherit?

Across Europe, parts of the nationalist right are increasingly blurring the distinction between culture and ethnicity. The result is a view of national identity where belonging depends on where a person’s ancestors come from.
This way of thinking is called ethnonationalism – where membership of a nation depends on ethnic background or ancestry, rather than simply on citizenship or cultural identity.

In Denmark, where I live, this idea has recently taken a striking turn. A few months ago, I appeared in a televised debate opposite a former political adviser to a Danish right-wing party who, in essence and quite seriously, argued that to be Danish, you have to be able to tolerate milk.

The argument draws on the fact that the ability to digest lactose, the sugar in milk, is more common among people with Northern European ancestry. The suggestion was that this biological trait could help define who is truly Danish.

Others on the nationalist right soon made similar arguments. One commentator wrote that Danish ancestry should be the basis for defining Danishness, because cultural “spirit” ultimately derives from blood.
But while the ability to digest milk might seem an absurd test of Danishness, the underlying question is a serious one and it extends far beyond Denmark.
When citizenship isn’t enough

Similar ideas are gaining ground elsewhere in Europe. In France, Marine Le Pen’s nationalist political project has promoted an ethnonationalist view of national identity, in which ancestry plays a central role in defining who belongs.

While Germany’s far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) has also made ethnonationalist claims as it has gained ground. In 2025, Germany’s domestic intelligence agency classified the party as right-wing extremist, although the legal status and implications of that classification have been contested.

These movements differ, but they raise a common question: can someone be a citizen of a country, live there for years and participate in its society, yet still be considered an outsider because of their ancestry?
This distinction between legal citizenship and supposedly authentic national belonging is central to the nationalist right’s calls for “remigration” across Europe.

The term is used by proponents to argue that people with migrant backgrounds should be removed from countries where they live, even when they have citizenship or were born there. This can include calling for the mass deportation of people deemed not to belong to the nation because of their ethnicity, ancestry or cultural background.

Such ideas often overlap with the so-called “great replacement” conspiracy theory, which claims those with non-Western backgrounds are replacing existing populations. And elements of this narrative have been adopted by nationalist and far-right politicians across Europe.

The word “ethnocultural” brings together two ideas: that a nation has a distinctive culture and that this culture belongs to a particular ethnic group. It suggests that national identity is not simply something people can learn or participate in, but something rooted in their origins.

Some researchers describe the shift in how nationalist politicians talk about national identity as a “cultural turn”. Rather than focusing explicitly on race or ancestry, they increasingly talk about protecting a country’s culture, values and way of life.

On the surface, that might sound more inclusive; people can learn the language or adopt new customs. But if a country’s culture is treated as something you inherit from your ancestors, rather than something you can share and take part in, the boundary between insiders and outsiders remains.

My research in Denmark has examined how national identity has changed over time. The findings suggest that, despite what some nationalist political groups argue, most people do not see ancestry as the defining feature of national belonging.

The Danish Values Study, part of a wider European survey, asks people about their beliefs and values. Comparing responses from the most recent 2008 and 2017 surveys, the proportion who thought being Danish was mainly about having Danish roots fell from 19% to 15%.

Meanwhile, around four in five saw being Danish as a matter of belonging to the country and its society rather than having a particular ethnic background. This figure remained almost unchanged, at 77% in 2008 and 79% in 2017. These findings offer a different perspective from the idea that national identity is rooted in blood (or milk).

This understanding also has roots in history. The Danish theologian NFS Grundtvig expressed a vision of national belonging in his 1848 poem Folkeligheden: “To a people all belong, who count themselves as part of it”. In other words, belonging is something people can claim for themselves, rather than something dictated by family background.

That said, the poem has featured in debates about Danish identity, with figures on the right using it to argue for a narrower definition of national belonging, while others see it as an argument for a more inclusive idea of Danishness.

And ultimately this raises the broader question: who has the legitimacy to define who belongs to a country or not? A question that will likely be a defining feature of European politics for years to come.

articles.title: UK appoints new climate security envoy – here’s what she could change
articles.author: James Dyke, Assistant Director of the Global Systems Institute, University of Exeter
paras: The UK government has just appointed Madeleine Alessandri as the world’s first special representative for climate security.

Prime minister Andy Burnham announced the new role in his speech at the UN climate summit, Cop31, in Turkey. This, he said, would be part of “a new era of British leadership on climate”. He also cited climate as “a national security issue” – a sign that Burnham considers this environmental crisis a significant risk to the country’s social stability and economy.
With a remit to “support ministers to champion UK leadership on climate and nature security”, Alessandri will report to the foreign secretary.

Climate change has long been considered as a threat multiplier because it compounds and increases many risks to national security. Unfortunately, many governments have failed to acknowledge such threats, resulting in a dangerous blind spot.

For example, a warmer world will produce more erratic weather that will impact harvests. Less food produces price spikes. In order to try to ensure food security, governments implement export controls. This can cause globally traded food prices to spike driving people into food poverty, exacerbate tensions and lead to conflict.
The 2026 UK harvest is the worst on record. Four of the five worst harvests have happened since 2020. This puts further pressure on UK farmers.

As climate security envoy, one of Alessandri’s priorities will need to be the state of national food security. That’s because the UK imports 40% of the food it consumes and so is extremely exposed to the tightening of global food supply.

Given that this year’s super El Niño (when certain parts of the Pacific are warmer than usual) is already creating havoc around the world, Alessandri may soon find herself embroiled in efforts to ensure that the responses to the consequences of the climate crisis do not make the situation worse.

Responding to extreme weather and climate consequences can produce derailment risks whereby efforts to reduce climate change get blown off course by escalating climate and social destabilisation. For example, in response to rising food insecurity national governments can ban food exports. This increases food prices even further. Protests over the cost of living can spiral into wider unrest. All this can make it difficult to maintain the political will required to progress the energy transition.

Alessandri is a career civil servant and the former chair of the UK’s joint intelligence committee (JIC) which oversees the UK’s secret intelligence services. Until now, the security implications of climate change sat within Katie White’s remit as the UK’s minister for climate transition in the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero.

It is perhaps no coincidence that it was the JIC that commissioned the previously supressed report on the national security implications of climate change. While published by the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs, it is widely acknowledged that the national security assessment on global ecosystems was produced by the JIC while Allesandri was leading it.

She will now be in a position to negotiate directly with other nations and organisations specifically about the food and wider security impacts of climate change. I would expect other governments to create similar roles in the near future because climate change is rapidly rising up the ranks of issues that are relevant to national security.

articles.title: The ‘religious left’ may be rising – but Black Christian women have been there all along
articles.author: Dara Delgado, Assistant Professor of Religion, University of North Carolina Wilmington
paras: During campaign season, headlines were full of candidates who spoke openly about their faith – and many of them were Democrats.

Adam Hamilton, the new senator-elect from Kansas, is pastor of the United States’ largest United Methodist congregation. Frederick Haynes, who will represent a Texas district in the U.S. House of Representatives, is a Baptist pastor. Texas Sen.-elect James Talarico is a Presbyterian seminary student who put a biblical commandment – “Love thy neighbor” – at the center of his campaign.

Since election night, journalists and commentators have attributed a significant amount of credit for the proverbial “Blue Wave” to the religious left. Although some mention Michigan Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed, who is Muslim, and Ohio Gov.-elect Amy Acton, who is Jewish, the focus has been on progressive Christians.

As a scholar of race, gender and religion whose work focuses on Black Protestant Christianity, I found post-election reporting about a rise in the religious left curious. Voters from many faith traditions did help power the “Blue Wave,” but one often-overlooked group has long been the left’s staunchest supporters: Black Christian women.

Focus on the “return” of the religious Democrats highlights the contrast between the religious diversity on the left and the allegiance between MAGA Republicans and evangelicals on the right. According to NBC exit polls, 82% of voters who consider themselves white evangelicals or born-again Christians voted for GOP candidates in 2026. In 2024, 82% of evangelicals in 10 key states voted for President Donald Trump.

But talking about religious Democrats as if they are a new, shiny bauble implies that, until this election, religious progressives have been off the ballot. That is simply not the case, especially when it comes to Black women.

Over the last four elections, majorities of both female voters and Black voters have voted blue. Black women vote for Democrats by an ever bigger margin: 93%, in 2026 exit polls, compared with 59% of women overall and 86% of Black men. Although Black women account for only 5-7% of Americans, they have been the most consistent Democratic voting bloc.

More than 7 in 10 Black Americans are Christian, and the vast majority are Protestant. Another 4% belong to other faiths, including Islam, and 22% are religiously unaffiliated. According to Pew’s 2023-24 Religious Landscape Survey, 2 in 3 members of Black Protestant denominations are women.
Many Black women candidates spoke about faith on the campaign trail.

For example, Keisha Lance Bottoms, the governor-elect of Georgia, attends a Methodist church. A few days after her victory, she spoke at the historic Ebenezer Baptist Church in Atlanta, pastored by Democratic Sen. Raphael Warnock of Georgia. During her visit, Lance Bottoms recalled that she had prayed about whether to run for governor and said that “God told me to go.” Her billionaire opponent was a “Goliath,” she said, but “our God supplied all of our needs.”
Anita Earls, who was re-elected as a judge on the North Carolina Supreme Court, is a longtime member of the African Methodist Episcopal Church.

Among sitting Democrats, Delaware Sen. Lisa Blunt Rochester has spoken about her Christian faith. Massachusetts Rep. Ayanna Pressley, who grew up Baptist, has called herself “a sister in Christ and a woman of faith. Someone who believes in the power of prayer.”
Each of these women is part of the religious left.

Before them was Shirley Chisholm, who became the first Black woman elected to Congress in 1968. Four years later, she was the first Black woman to run for president on the Democratic ticket. Her 1970 memoir, “Unbought and Unbossed,” recounts her commitment to progressive ideals, ranging from education to women’s reproductive rights, and to her Christian faith.

“America has the laws and the material resources it takes to ensure justice for all its people,” she wrote. “What it lacks is the heart, the humanity, the Christian love that it would take. It is perhaps unrealistic to hope that I can help give this nation any of those things, but that is what I believe I have to try to do.”

Before Black women were voted into office, however, they were already pillars of progressive politics. Historically, Black churches have been more than a place to foster belief. They have also been community-based institutions that fostered social, political and economic justice.

Within Black denominations, men tend to hold senior leadership positions. In his famed book “The Souls of Black Folk,” sociologist W.E.B. DuBois observed that the Black preacher was also a community “leader, a politician, an orator, a ‘boss,’ an intriguer, an idealist.”

Women’s role was less public, but no less vital, including social and political organizing. In “Witnessing and Testifying,” religion professor Rosetta Ross showed how Black women’s faith and activism inspired each other during the Civil Rights Movement. Among the women Ross surveyed is Ella Baker, who organized the initial meeting for what would become the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee and often “used Christian scripture to admonish listeners to fight” for freedom.

Women like Baker, voting rights activist Fannie Lou Hamer, and Clara Muhammad, wife of Nation of Islam founder Elijah Muhammad, show how Black communities’ concerns and faith often intertwined with progressive politics. In 1958, Nannie Helen Burroughs, founder of the Women’s Auxiliary of the National Baptist Convention, said that African American Christians wanted “Jesus, jobs and justice.”
Black, Christian and progressive
Today, too, faith guides many progressive Black women’s politics and public service. For voting rights activists, for example, casting a ballot is not just a right, but something sacred.

Over the past week, journalists and political pundits have drawn attention to the many different groups that moved to the left to fuel Democrats’ midterm victories, including young voters, Latinos, Asian Americans, men and political independents. Black women voters, meanwhile, have remained steady.

Indeed, history has shown how their steadiness helped guide the Democratic Party’s political and moral compass. And I am willing to wager that they will continue to play an essential role in what the left does between now and 2028.

articles.title: Pa. Gov. Josh Shapiro’s popularity and ‘get sh-t done’ attitude might not cut it in crowded 2028 Democratic field – but he has options
articles.author: Alison Dagnes, Professor of Political & Social Inquiry, Shippensburg University
paras: The 2026 midterm elections swept Democrats into office around the country in such numbers that journalists were running out of synonyms for “massive.”

In Pennsylvania, Gov. Josh Shapiro won reelection by 22 percentage points, winning more than 60% of the vote – something that has been accomplished only twice before in the modern era in the Keystone State.

Not only did Shapiro wipe the floor with his opponent Stacy Garrity, the state treasurer, but he also helped flip four U.S. House seats from red to blue. His coattails benefited down-ballot candidates, helping Democrats solidify their control of the state House and flip the state Senate as well.
Shapiro’s political stock in Pennsylvania is riding high.

I’m a political science professor and political media researcher in central Pennsylvania, and many of my former students work in Harrisburg. Some are Democrats working for or around the governor; others are Republicans working in different corners of state government. All are finely tuned to the political gossip that swirls around a successful politician whose star is on the rise. It is the worst-kept secret in American politics that Josh Shapiro wants to be president.

I’ve met the governor a handful of times and can attest to his George Clooney-level charisma. He’s a hard worker, has maintained a remarkably clean political profile, and is from many accounts a genuinely nice dude.
And yet, there are plenty of reasons his ambitions may require some careful timing, regardless of his personal strengths.
A reputation for getting stuff done

Shapiro’s political victories didn’t just happen. Over the past four years, he has worked to demonstrate bipartisan competence as Pennsylvania’s chief executive, adopting an expression he uses frequently: “get sh-t done.”
Now, with Democrats holding the governor’s office and both chambers of the General Assembly, Shapiro told reporters: “We got the power now, the House, the Senate. We have to deliver.”

Shapiro’s approval ratings have remained strong, consistent with his reelection margins. That’s unusual in a state that has swung back and forth between supporting Donald Trump in 2016, Joe Biden in 2020 and Trump again in 2024, each time by fewer than 2 percentage points.
If Shapiro is indeed seriously eyeing the White House, his current popularity will certainly serve him well. But winning the presidency is an enormous undertaking, particularly in a crowded field.

With Trump unable to run in 2028, the next presidential election will feature open seats for both parties and likely attract many candidates. Democrats, in particular, have a deep bench of attractive potential contenders.

There are so many possibilities that Shapiro could find himself running against people very much like him: younger centrists, swing-state politicians and accomplished elected officials with solid records. Consider just a few names that could be part of the conversation: Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff, Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker and former Chicago Mayor Rahm Emanuel.

Shapiro would have to find a way to distinguish himself in a field filled with candidates who can make many of the same arguments about their experience, political appeal and accomplishments. That’s a tall order. A Plan B might be wise.
Options beyond the White House
Fortunately for Shapiro, other choices abound.

He could run for the Senate in 2028 against incumbent John Fetterman, if Fetterman seeks reelection. This would be a twofer: Shapiro would continue his rise in politics, and he would likely beat a guy he apparently does not like. The two reportedly don’t speak, much less get along.

Shapiro could also position himself for a vice presidential nomination by attaching himself to another 2028 hopeful. This would buy him time to build his national profile, allow the presidential field to sort itself out and potentially put him in a strong position for another run at the White House down the road. It would also give him an opportunity to demonstrate that he can work effectively on a national stage.

Or he could angle for a Cabinet post. The federal government has undergone significant restructuring under DOGE and Trump’s executive orders. Should a Democrat win the White House in 2028, rebuilding federal agencies and restoring institutional capacity will be a monumental undertaking. Shapiro could be an attractive candidate for a major administrative role.

The bottom line for Shapiro is that he will need to distinguish himself from a crowded field of Democrats by emphasizing his statewide victories in a major swing state, impressive fundraising ability and a political voice that can evoke Barack Obama without alienating either his party or the broader electorate. That’s a tricky feat, even for the most talented politicians.

But Nov. 3, 2026, showed us that he knows how to make sh-t happen. Whatever he decides, the next two years will be important for Shapiro, consequential for Democrats, and fascinating for political scientists like me, who will be watching events unfold with a keen eye and, probably, a bucket of popcorn.
