articles.title: Democrats’ agenda will be set by their ability to organize and compromise — not by the socialist, progressive or centrist factions all claiming victory
articles.author: SoRelle Wyckoff Gaynor, Assistant Professor of Public Policy and Politics, University of Virginia
paras: The massive Democratic majority in the U.S. House and Senate that was ushered in by a historic blue midterm vote is an ideologically diverse one.

Candidates spent much of the past year differentiating their positions from the mainstream Democratic coalition. The result is a freshman class filled with as many progressive liberals as moderate problem solvers.

By the morning after Election Day, pundits and current Democratic members across the political spectrum were quick to claim their ideologically aligned candidates as the “majority makers” – the group most responsible for the large victory.
Centrist Democrats pointed to pragmatic moderates flipping Trump-won seats. Liberal voices highlighted the enthusiasm and turnout driven by a new, progressive vision.
As a result, days after the election the focus had turned toward January: Who will become the majority maker within Congress?

Party caucus leaders have already started building their roster: The Progressive Caucus claims at least 25 new members in their ranks, growing their membership to over 100 Democratic members. The moderate Blue Dog Caucus doubled in size, from 10 to 20 new members. And in the middle, the center-left New Dems are projecting a caucus of over 140 members.

I’m a political scientist who has worked in and now studies Congress. Figuring out the dynamics and direction of the 120th Congress requires looking at more than the ideological positions of the candidates who won. Instead, focusing on the number of candidates who won can provide insight into the direction of the party as a whole.

The large – and at the time of writing, still growing – margins of Democratic control in the 120th Congress are the biggest since 1993, before Congress became consistently competitive and increasingly polarized. Those large margins provide essential context for understanding how this new ideological coalition will work in Congress.

While history demonstrates that an ideologically diverse party can be hard to wrangle, the size of the new Democratic majority provides some breathing room for policy negotiation and procedural debates.

Unlike the current Republican Caucus that is reliant on keeping historically narrow majorities together to pass party goals, future Democratic leadership can stand to lose a few votes. With a minimum of 254 seats in the House and 54 seats in the Senate, small-scale Democratic defections are irrelevant.
This breathing room provides the potential for negotiation, while also limiting any mandate an ideological group may claim.

For instance, the 120th Congress will have eight members in the House who are backed or affiliated with the Democratic Socialists of America, known as the DSA. In raw terms of political power, when the majority has at least 36 votes to spare on any given party-line bill, this group may not matter in policymaking.
But big numbers do matter.

If a group – say, the entirety of the Progressive Caucus’ 100-plus membership – decides to stick together, leadership will be forced to listen. Thus, the potential power of ideological factions depends not only on their ideas but their own organizational skills.

When groups in Congress develop practices such as confidential meetings or binding rules that require members vote together on certain votes, the legitimacy of group demands can be strengthened. This is a strategy that has been employed with relative success by the far-right Republican Freedom Caucus since it was formed in 2014.
The overarching policy goals for newly elected Democrats are consistent across the ideological spectrum: lowering the cost of living and rooting out corruption.

This was highlighted in acceptance speeches by Democrats from South Carolina to Texas to Michigan. All emphasized the same policy-focused promise: Instead of fighting left versus right, the fight should focus on the top versus the bottom.
This shared vision is no doubt important. My research has shown that a cohesive message is a key part of winning and maintaining majority control.

However, the “blue tsunami” was powered by voters with very specific policy demands. And as is always the case with policymaking, the details matter. Does healthcare reform mean reinstating the Obamacare subsidies set to expire on Jan. 1, 2027? Or does it mean something bolder, such as Medicare for All?
While there is power in numbers, the organizational strength and ultimate success of ideological groups in Congress depends on how unified they can be around specific policy goals and proposals.
First hurdle: Pick a leader
This means that who is doing the unifying also matters.
The success of any potential legislative package heavily relies on congressional leaders’ knowledge of congressional rules and their willingness to incorporate member viewpoints.

This necessity of having leadership in place to get legislation moving is epitomized by the order of operations for a new congressional session. In the coming weeks, both parties will hold closed-door, secret-ballot elections to select their new party leaders. That’s well before any legislation is even drafted.

With a Democratic caucus filled with anti-establishment candidates across the ideological spectrum, and external pressure from political pundits to dump current Democratic leadership, the future of the Democratic Party has been projected onto this otherwise ritualistic vote.

But the power and success of congressional leadership lies in its procedural acumen, not its ideological vision. Some already in Congress have noted New York Democratic Rep. Hakeem Jeffries’ experience and working relationships in discussions of whether he should be house speaker. Furthermore, groups can extract concessions during leadership selection in exchange for their support, such as seats on powerful committees or an agreement on policy agenda items.

Sen. Chuck Schumer, the longtime New York lawmaker aiming to lead Senate Democrats again, faces more public criticism from his party. While no one has yet stepped up as an alternative, momentum is building for Maryland Sen. Chris Van Hollen, who has said he is “in listening mode.”

To external observers, the selection of party leadership seems like a defining point for the party. But whether a new caucus translates to new leaders or new rules ultimately depends on the organizational power of new members and their already-serving co-workers – and what a party leader can offer them in terms of policy goals and procedural capabilities. Who is chosen as leader is not necessarily a signal of what the party’s policy goals will be.

That picture is not yet clear – and it may not be for some time. After all, the new Democratic margins in Congress are a result of a collection of majority makers. The margins of victory tell a story about more than presidential backlash. Across the country, progressive enthusiasm and moderate appeal turned voters toward the Democratic Party. And while everything is local, national enthusiasm matters, too.

The 120th Congress will include progressives and moderates and the establishment candidates in the middle that are all required parts of the same whole. Or as political scientist E.E. Schattschneider argued in 1960 in his seminal work “The Semisovereign People,” it would be a mistake to give credit to one group for the success of an election. Rather, achieving a consequential majority in America requires coalition building – and maintenance.

SoRelle Wyckoff Gaynor does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organization that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

articles.title: After midterm rout, Republicans can still confirm a Supreme Court justice, but at what cost?
articles.author: Paul M. Collins Jr., Professor of Legal Studies and Political Science, UMass Amherst
paras: The 2026 midterm rout that awarded Democrats decisive majorities in the Senate and House has also sparked interest in the future of the U.S. Supreme Court.

With Democrats securing at least a 54-seat majority in the Senate on Jan. 3, 2027, the window is rapidly closing for President Donald Trump to appoint a new Supreme Court justice and safeguard conservative dominance on the court for decades.

As a Supreme Court scholar, I know that judicial appointments have real consequences. Look no further than Roe v. Wade: Within two years of securing a 6–3 conservative majority, the high court in 2022 eliminated the constitutional right to abortion that had existed for almost 50 years.
Now that Democrats have taken the Senate, if a Republican-appointed justice retires before Jan. 3, it will trigger one of the most explosive confirmation battles in American history.
Here’s how the fight is likely to play out – and why the stakes are so high.
Who is most likely to retire?

Justices Samuel Alito and Clarence Thomas top the list of potential retirees after Democrats won the Senate – even if Alito has reportedly said he will not retire immediately. Alito and Thomas are the court’s oldest justices, at 76 and 78, respectively. Thomas is the court’s longest-serving justice, appointed by President George H.W. Bush in 1991.

Perhaps more importantly, both justices have deep ties to the conservative legal movement. This is a network of lawyers, judges and politicians who seek to etch conservative principles into law. Overturning Roe v. Wade was at the top of the conservative wish list.
My research suggests that both Alito and Thomas care about their legacies. And they both understand that a Democratic-controlled Senate will block another Trump-appointed nominee.

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer made this clear just days after the midterms. And in October 2026, Senate Judiciary Committee member Richard Blumenthal, the Democrat from Connecticut, said, “It is slim to none that we would support a nominee from this administration.”
Though Alito has indicated he intends to stay on the court through its 2026 term, Thomas has made no recent public statements about retirement. And Alito is free to change his mind at any time.

If Alito or Thomas announce their retirement soon, Republicans would have enough time to confirm a successor. The Senate has four and a half work weeks scheduled between Election Day and Jan. 3. Justice Amy Coney Barrett was confirmed less than a month after her nomination, making the timeline tight but doable.

Democrats will likely attempt to slow down the process, but they face an uphill battle with few options. Republicans stripped away key delaying tactics in recent years by ending the filibuster in 2017 and ignoring the Judiciary Committee’s quorum rules in 2020. This rule requires nine members be present to transact business, including two members of the minority party.
A potentially historic battle
A Republican effort to confirm a Supreme Court nominee during a lame-duck Senate would spark a historic battle with Democrats.

Democrats would surely point to how Republicans handled President Barack Obama’s appointment of Merrick Garland in 2016. A seat on the court opened up after conservative Antonin Scalia died on Feb. 13, almost nine months before the November presidential election.

Republicans refused to move Garland’s nomination through the confirmation process, using their majority power to set the Senate’s agenda. This marked the first time since 1866 that a Supreme Court nomination that was not withdrawn failed to receive an up-or-down vote in the Senate.

To justify this, Republicans created the so-called “McConnell Rule,” named after former Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell of Kentucky. According to McConnell, the Senate should not fill Supreme Court vacancies “in the middle of a presidential election year.”
Four years later, Senate Republicans abruptly abandoned the rule. This allowed them to push through Coney Barrett’s confirmation just days before the 2020 presidential election.
Democrats did not take kindly to this reversal.
Schumer pulled no punches in a speech the day of Barrett’s confirmation vote. Schumer said the day “will go down as one of the darkest days in the 231-year history of the United States Senate.”

He alleged the Republican majority made “a mockery of its own stated principle – that the American people deserve a voice in the selection of Supreme Court Justices – completing the partisan theft of two seats on the Supreme Court using completely contradictory rationales.”
Democrats were clearly outraged by what they saw as two stolen Supreme Court seats.
However, I believe that pushing through a nominee will trigger an even fiercer fight. Senate Democrats will see such a confirmation as a power grab that sidelines the voice of voters.
Furthermore, if a Republican justice retires after the midterms, the move will almost certainly be viewed as purely partisan.

This has the potential to further erode public support for the court, which is sitting near historic lows. And it will likely fuel the fire of Supreme Court reform, including the possibility of expanding the number of justices on the court.
Put simply, in securing a short-term conservative victory, Republicans may end up handing Democrats the exact justification they need to reshape the high court.
This is an updated version of an article originally published on Oct. 14, 2026.

articles.title: America’s 2-party system seems weird, but adding a 3rd party could make voter representation worse
articles.author: Robin E. Best, Professor of Political Science, Binghamton University, State University of New York
paras: In most races in the midterm elections on Nov. 3, 2026, Americans had only two realistic choices: Democrats and Republicans.

As a scholar of parties and elections, I am often asked why the U.S. has only two major parties, while other democracies offer voters three, four or even five choices. The U.S. system looks weird compared to those, but that isn’t necessarily a bad thing.

The two “umbrella” Democratic and Republican parties mask many underlying differences in political preferences, but this large and fluid two-party system may represent voters at least as well as Canada and the United Kingdom do. Those countries elect members of their lower legislative house in the same way as the U.S., but, as my research suggests, their additional parties can distort representation.

An electoral system is the set of rules that determine how votes translate into elected representatives. The U.S. uses what’s called a single-member district plurality, or an SMD-p system, which means each district elects only one representative, and whoever gets the most votes wins.

This “winner-take-all” system is different from proportional representation, the electoral system used by most other democracies. In that system, several representatives are elected in each district, and a party’s share of seats roughly matches its share of the vote – for example, a party winning 40% of the votes would get around 40% of the seats.

SMD-p systems encourage stiff competition between two parties in each district. Because the system gives losing parties nothing, it discourages voters from supporting third parties that have no chance of winning. There is no rule against having more than two parties, but why vote for a party that is sure to lose? With only one possible winner in each district, there are typically only two real competitors.

There are many possible reasons the U.S. does not have a viable third party. The presidency pushes politicians to run under one of the major labels, and state ballot access laws make it harder for minor-party candidates to get on the ballot.
Another reason is the nature of the two parties themselves.

As “umbrella” parties, the Democrats and Republicans mask underlying differences in political preferences. For example, the Pew Research Center identifies nine ideological subtypes of American voters, including Faith First Conservatives, Pragmatic and Polite Right, Loyal Liberals and Leftward Progressives.

In a different country, with different electoral rules, these nine groups could form multiple political parties. In the U.S., they must choose between Republicans and Democrats. Democrats, for example, unite what Pew calls the Order and Opportunity Left, the Left-Out Left, the Loyal Liberals and the Leftward Progressives.
The same umbrella effect shows up in Congress.

Congressional Democrats and Republicans have typically had lower levels of party unity – the extent to which party members vote the same way on legislation – than their European counterparts. This lack of unity is often viewed negatively. In the 1950s, a group of political scientists representing the American Political Science Association, frustrated with how fluid the parties’ positions could be, called for more unified ones that would provide voters with clear and consistent options.
But low unity has an upside: It gives politicians the flexibility to represent their own voters, even when those voters disagree with the rest of the party.
More parties, less representation
So why not add another party or two to the American system?
One metric political scientists use to evaluate representation is electoral disproportionality: the gap between parties’ vote shares and their seat shares.

The U.S. electoral system is one of the most disproportional that democracies use, since only the district winner is represented. But that disproportionality rarely shows up when only two parties compete.

On the other hand, other democracies using the same kind of electoral system as the U.S., such as Canada and the U.K., have several parties competing, which sometimes poses problems for good representation.

One example of this was the U.K.’s 2024 general election, which produced some of the most disproportional results in British history. Multiparty competition allowed the Labour Party to win more than 63% of the seats in the House of Commons with less than 34% of the vote. Meanwhile, Reform UK received 14% of the vote and won less than 1% of seats.
Imagine a country with 10 districts, each electing one legislator. Only two parties run: the Purple Party and the Yellow Party.

The Purple Party wins six districts and Yellow wins four. Purple gets about 56% of the vote and takes 60% of the seats. Yellow gets about 44% of the vote and takes 40% of the seats. In each case, the gap between vote share and seat share is about 4 points. That is considered the measure of disproportionality.

Now imagine a third party, the Green Party, enters the race. It wins 30% of the vote in each district, taking more votes from the Purple Party than from Yellow. That costs Purple any districts it had previously won narrowly. Now, Yellow wins six districts and Purple wins four.
Three things happen when the third party enters the race.
First, the winning party changes. Now, the Yellow Party wins a majority of seats – 60% – with just over a third of the vote.
Second, despite receiving 30% of the vote across all districts, and often coming in second place, the Green Party does not win any seats at all.
Third, disproportionality increases from 4 points to 28. Only Purple, with 40% of the seats on just under 36% of the vote, comes close to proportionality.
Adding a third party flips the winning party from one to the other and increases disproportionality, and this all happens without that third party winning a single seat.

My research suggests that in countries using the SMD-p system, growing support for third parties has increased disproportionality, sometimes dramatically. The U.S. is the exception: Its two-party system keeps disproportionality low, often even lower than in countries that use proportional representation.

The large and fluid two-party system in the U.S. may represent voters at least as well as systems with viable third parties. The only way out without further distorting representation would be to change the electoral system to some version of proportional representation. Nothing in the Constitution prevents that.
Americans have valid complaints about their parties, and there are ways to address them. But simply adding more parties to the mix is unlikely to solve anything.

articles.title: Media ultimately exposed Russell Brand – but his fame and celebrity added to victims’ trauma
articles.author: Lindsey Blumell, Lecturer in Journalism, City St George's, University of London
paras: After years of caution, journalists can now exchange the word “alleged” for “convicted” when describing Russell Brand as a sexual predator. Following a four-week trial, where six women testified in detail, the former comedian was jailed for ten years and six months for one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault. He was cleared of two further counts of rape and one of attempted indecent assault.

When sentencing Brand, Justice Joel Bennathan emphasised the women’s courage for coming forward. Four victim impact statements were read to the court, one of them by the victim herself, before Brand was sentenced. All four women discussed the deep and lasting impact of their assaults, highlighting the role of the media in their trauma.

Complainant three stated how difficult it was to see Brand for years “being celebrated for his disgusting behaviour against women, like it was all a joke”. She also described how seeing the news coverage of the story caused her to have the only panic attack of her life.

Complainant four said she suffered heavy anxiety watching the coverage. And complainant five said she was “unprepared for the level of publicity”, adding: “It has been extremely distressing to relive what happened and see it discussed so widely.”

Complainant six, who was working for Channel 4 at the time she was attacked, stated she reported her sexual assault to the broadcaster, which had recruited Brand to work on a project. But she said of her complaint: “It was brushed under the carpet by senior management.”

The trial is an example of the role media can play in uplifting the career of powerful people like Brand. This is both through platforming celebrities in “puff” articles and TV segments, as well as in their failure to act on reports of unprofessional and illegal behaviour.
Yet it was the investigative reporting by Channel 4 and The Times and The Sunday Times in 2023 that the Metropolitan Police credit for starting an investigation into Brand.
In fact, most of the high-profile cases of sexual violence that have gone to trial in the UK and US have included journalistic exposés.

Uncovering the sexual violence of high-profile people is time-consuming and risky for news organisations. Chief news correspondent for The Sunday Times Rosamund Urwin and investigations correspondent for The Times Charlotte Wace said they worked on the Brand story for nearly four years before publishing. They contacted more than 500 sources in the process.

Since the trial, they have discussed how surprised they were that Brand’s defence team centred their news reporting throughout the proceedings. “Our reporting, while important as the catalyst for some of them, wasn’t on trial,” Urwin later said in a TV interview.

The attempts to undermine the news reporting even seeped out of the courtroom. Urwin was confronted by Brand’s barrister Ian Winter KC on the day the verdicts were returned. She introduced herself – because the barrister had mentioned her reporting frequently in court. He reportedly replied: “I hope you’re pleased with yourself”. Urwin responded: “I’m pleased justice has been done”, to which Winter is said to have retorted: “Well, it wasn’t. You f***** it … Congratulations.” Winter has now referred himself to regulator the Bar Standards Board.
Women accusing a high-profile man can face anger, either online or in person. Brand’s father Ron even said after the sentencing that his son is the real victim – not the women accusing him.
Journalists also face contempt through threats of “strategic litigation against public participation” or Slapps – lawsuits that are increasingly being used to suppress reporting in the UK and US.

And it doesn’t stop at Slapps. TV personality and author David Walliams recently attempted to block a joint ITV News and Guardian investigation that includes several women alleging sexual misconduct. Two accusers say they were 15 years old when they met Walliams. He filed an injunction, which was dismissed by the high court, meaning he could then be named. Walliams denies the allegations against him.

In 2020, the actor Johnny Depp tried and failed to sue The Sun newspaper for reporting he was a “wife beater” (although he was successful in a US case against his former wife Amber Heard). In 2003, Jeffery Epstein successfully used threats to pressure Vanity Fair magazine to water down its coverage of him. And in 2017, disgraced film producer Harvey Weinstein allegedly managed to stop NBC from publishing an investigation into his sexual misconduct. The probe was eventually published by The New Yorker.

But despite instances like these, powerful celebrities like Brand can hide in plain sight for years with the help of news media organisations. The relationship can be mutually beneficial. Celebrities are legitimised and hyped through regular attention – and in return, news outlets get clicks and views.

This relationship can sour if news organisations invest in the lengthy and complicated process of uncovering sexual crimes. In the process, it’s still the accusers, often victims of sexual crimes, who endure years of anxiety and scrutiny.
Lindsey Blumell receives funding from City, St.George's University of London.

articles.title: Andy Burnham and climate change: where does the prime minister really stand?
articles.author: James Jackson, Lecturer and Research Fellow, School of Social Sciences, University of Manchester
paras: Since becoming prime minister, Andy Burnham has set out a relatively ambitious political agenda. He has outlined plans for a national care service, a “Great British Grid” and suggested a rethink of the UK’s relationship with the European Union.
But one big omission of Burnham’s agenda is climate policy. Amid the proposals that put clear water between him and his predecessor Keir Starmer, Burnham’s climate agenda remains unknown.

The prime minister has reiterated his intention to reach net zero by 2050 (though this target is contentious due to whether it actually reflects climate science as well as the extent to which it depends upon as yet unavailable technology). He has also pledged to attend Cop31, the UN climate summit currently underway in Turkey, in person. However, the budget – Burnham’s first real opportunity to set out his vision – raised concerns about whether his political rhetoric could translate into a coherent climate policy.

The budget revealed that increased defence spending would come at the cost of £3 billion of cuts at the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero. Subsidies for heat pumps, boilers, the warm homes plan, hydrogen and carbon capture and storage were the most prominent policies to be culled. This not only limits the UK’s green industrial policy, but suggests that energy security is still not considered to be part of national security.
Energy security and rising bills

For years, the UK has been misaligned with its own carbon budgets set under the Climate Change Act 2008. After the Conservatives began to question the objective of net zero towards the end of their term in office, the election of the first Labour government in 14 years was expected to mark a turning point.

Burnham’s climate position has become entwined (and somewhat undermined) by energy security concerns following the so-called fossilflationary pressures caused by the the US and Israel’s conflict with Iran. This has fed into the licensing of the Jackdaw gasfield 150 miles east of Aberdeen. This is part of Burnham’s self-described “pragmatic” approach to new drilling in the North Sea.

The initial justification was that the move would improve energy security by increasing the domestic supply of oil and gas. But critics say that increasing supply has little to no effect on domestic bills, as prices are set by international markets. Revenues made from the project will be used to finance an Energy Wealth Fund to invest in green technologies elsewhere.

Then there’s the cost of living. As winter approaches, an increasing number of households will have to choose between heating and eating. In response, Chancellor John Healey’s budget removed green levies from consumer bills. These levies fund environmental programmes such as renewable schemes, but the money will now be sourced from general taxation.
This does reduce bills in the short term. But the shift, combined with other cuts, raises doubts over the long term.

It’s argued that removing green levies from bills will reduce the relative cost of energy. This is a salient argument as the UK approaches a period of higher energy demand to heat the country’s homes. But critics say that reducing support for green energy infrastructure will delay the advent of abundant cheap energy.
Political and economic tests

Labour now has two challenges. The first is the political bind the party finds itself in. Its manifesto does not contain anything resembling an ambitious climate policy. Although Burnham represents a change at the top, he has not won the right to depart from the platform upon which Starmer was elected.
Whether this represents a constraint on Burnham’s political vision or just more of the same on a limited climate policy is up for debate.

The second is an economic bind due to the UK’s tight fiscal position. This is despite taxation being at a historically high level – much of which has come from “fiscal drag” as taxpayers are pulled into higher tax bands.

The broader issues are that ten-year UK gilt yields – the rate the government pays on its debt – have risen to 5.13%. The irony of the rise in gilt yields is that they have increased primarily because of “fossilflation” as supply-side shocks have fed into energy prices.
As a result, the Bank of England has raised interest rates for the first time in three years, to 4%. This will further increase borrowing costs and make life less affordable for UK households.

And yet Labour’s propositions only put its climate policy into further doubt. It remains to be seen whether it will grant a licence for the Rosebank oil field, west of Shetland, which is larger than Jackdaw. Unless the government bends to political pressure, Burnham and energy secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh could make the same arguments about energy security again.

In the meantime, Burnham has signalled his desire to raise tariffs on Chinese green technology to align the UK more closely to the EU. This would be a bid to answer security worries, but tariffs on the cheapest and largest source of green technology places climate second to geopolitical concerns.
Under Burnham, climate policy has, at best, been lost amid the prime minister’s broader political platform. At worst, he has concluded it is a price worth paying to achieve his other objectives.

articles.title: What happens after a midterm tsunami? Lessons from 1974 and 1994
articles.author: Robert A. Strong, Senior Fellow, Miller Center, University of Virginia
paras: There were lots of surprises on the evening of Nov. 3 when the picture of the Democratic midterm success began to be painted on network news touch screens.
The maps kept getting bluer. Eventually, it was clear that this was not an ordinary midterm cycle when the party out of power slaps the wrist of the sitting president and his administration.
It was much bigger than that, something on a scale the U.S. has seen only two times in the past half-century.
One was the Newt Gingrich “revolution” in 1994 that put Republicans in control of the House of Representatives for the first time in 40 years.
The other was the election of 1974 that flooded Capitol Hill with “Watergate babies” – new members elected just after the Nixon-era scandals.
In both cases there were high hopes that big changes would take place in the aftermath of remarkable midterm elections. The actual results were more modest than the victors expected.

The 1994 midterm elections gave the Republican Party a dramatic victory. The Democrats lost their majority in the Senate, and 54 seats were flipped in the House of Representatives, making Gingrich the first Republican speaker of the House since Eisenhower lived in the White House.
It was a wipeout election that had not been expected, and it changed the dynamics of Democrat Bill Clinton’s presidency.

The combative Gingrich emerged as a political celebrity; partisanship intensified and gridlock became the new norm. Confrontations over spending led to controversial government shutdowns and the first modern threat to default on America’s debt obligations.
Because the new Republican congressional majorities appeared to overreach in their efforts to cut taxes and spending, Clinton was able to recover sufficient popularity to win a second term.

In the run-up to his bid for reelection, Clinton took the electoral rebuke of 1994 to heart and followed a centrist strategy that represented a move to the right of longtime Democratic positions on welfare, crime and immigration. He continued to oppose many Republican policy proposals but worked with Republicans to craft welfare reform legislation and new bills dealing with crime and immigration. Budget confrontation eventually gave way to compromise, and for a few years in the late 1990s the United States had a balanced budget.
Partisanship became more personal in Clinton’s second term when Gingrich pushed for impeachment following the revelations of the president’s affair with Monica Lewinsky.
Clinton, with a tarnished reputation, survived his Senate trial. Ironically, it was Gingrich who resigned after failing to remove the president at the ballot box or in the impeachment process.
Gingrich, the biggest winner in the 1994 midterms, left office with a promised revolution largely unrealized.
1974’s Watergate reformers
Going back even further in American political history, the midterm elections following President Richard Nixon’s resignation after the Watergate scandal produced a Democratic Party victory.
That victory was not a surprise; the scale of it was.

Democrats, who already had majorities in the House and Senate, won a huge margin in the congressional popular vote and brought new members to both chambers who were younger, more liberal and reform-minded.

They wanted to prevent future Watergates. New laws would make the government more open, more honest and more accountable. New and more staff would allow Congress to be less reliant on executive branch information and better able to act in foreign policy and budget management. Special prosecutors would be appointed to investigate abuses of power and violations of law.
A Democrat, Jimmy Carter, would be elected president two years after the massive 1974 midterm victory, and more reform legislation would be passed.

The post-Watergate congressional agenda was long and bold – the war powers resolution, a freedom of information act, the creation of inspectors general, campaign finance reform, a presidential records act and new legislation to regulate foreign intelligence surveillance and the bribing of foreign officials.
These new laws were supposed to stop, or uncover, the kind of wrongdoing that made Nixon an imperial president.
The new laws and institutions certainly made a difference – but not without creating their own problems.

All the post-Watergate presidents thought the war powers resolution was unconstitutional, objecting to its restrictions on the president’s authority as commander in chief, and U.S. military interventions overseas continued to occur. Special prosecutors conducted many investigations, but often at great expense and without adequate supervision or meaningful results.
Carter, narrowly elected president in 1976, served only one term and lost reelection to Ronald Reagan, who fully restored the Republican Party’s dominance in presidential politics.
Over time, many presidents, especially Donald Trump, dismantled or ignored important elements of the post-Watergate reforms.
The large and enthusiastic congressional majorities that took power after the 1974 midterms were energetic but produced a political legacy with complicated and controversial results.
Chaos and conflict – or compromise?
What is the country likely to see in the next few months and the next two years?

Will it be chaos, conflict and occasional compromise, like the politics that followed the midterms in 1994? Or will it be earnest and sometimes heavy-handed congressional efforts to investigate and prevent presidential wrongdoing, like those that swept through Washington after 1974?
Surprising midterm elections that create new majorities on Capitol Hill look to be revolutions in the days after they occur. Years later, they often appear to be more complex – and less significant.

articles.title: Voters rejected data centers in dozens of communities, fueling the narrative that opposition to the AI infrastructure contributed to the 2026 blue wave
articles.author: Barbara A. Trish, Professor of Political Science, Grinnell College
paras: Data centers were on the ballot, both directly and indirectly, in the 2026 midterm elections.
A total of 41 local ballot initiatives concerning data centers in 10 states were up for a vote. All but one resulted in measures to restrict or limit their development.

The centers also may have played a role in several high-profile contests. In Ohio’s race for a U.S. Senate seat, Democratic challenger Sherrod Brown hammered incumbent Jon Husted for his past support of data centers. In Texas, Gina Hinojosa made Republican Gov. Greg Abbott’s track record of supporting tax breaks for data centers a focal point of her winning campaign. Her victory marked a historic break with decades of Republican control in the state. As governor-elect, she immediately reaffirmed her campaign pledge to pursue legislation protecting Texans from data centers.

According to NBC exit poll data, 56% of voters felt that data centers were a major or even a crucial factor in influencing their congressional vote. For Black voters, the share was even higher, at 68%.

Data centers are key components in artificial intelligence infrastructure, housing the computing resources used to train AI models. These massive facilities guzzle energy and water and are very noisy. Many Americans argue that their costs, in terms of land use, higher utility bills and environmental degradation, outweigh the benefits.

I’m a professor of political science who studies political parties, electoral politics and technology. My forthcoming book, “Democratic Intelligence: Navigating Electoral Politics in an AI World,” examines how the adoption of this technology is reshaping established practices and power dynamics in campaigns.

Before the midterms, it had already appeared to be disrupting some partisan alignments. Following those historic elections, which have thoroughly shaken up America’s political geography, the widespread pushback against data centers is now part of the narrative explaining the dramatic results of the 2026 midterms.
Disrupting political polarization

In contrast to many other issues, concern about data centers is relatively bipartisan. The Annenberg Public Policy Center asked Americans in mid-2026 whether they support or oppose having data centers in their communities. Opposition was stronger among Democrats, at 69%, than Republicans, at 54%, but it crossed party lines.

Local ballot measures restricting data centers also cut across traditional political alignments. Communities as disparate as deeply red Edgewater, Florida, and solidly blue Alhambra, California, voted to prohibit them. The margins for the restrictions were large, averaging 49 percentage points.

The one restrictive local measure that failed to pass was in Harwood, North Dakota, population around 800. With a data center project already in progress, political and economic leaders prevailed in arguing that restrictions would cut into local revenue and stifle economic development more generally.

Exit polls taken during the midterm elections also detected a degree of bipartisanship. Of the 56% of voters who said data centers played a “major” or “crucial” role in their vote, approximately two-thirds were Democrats and one-third Republicans. Exit polls, however, should be interpreted with care, given their methodological limitations.
These responses hint at why the narrative that opposition to data centers helped fuel the Democrats’ historic midterm victory emerged right away.

The seeds of this argument were in place before the election, picking up on unusual alliances that marked the data center opposition. In cities and counties, zoning fights are drawing a diverse kind of resistance: environmentalists, voters reeling under high electricity costs, local-control advocates and farmers concerned that data centers eat up land. They unite in opposition to projects backed by powerful corporate interests.

Some of the bipartisanship around this issue has even seeped into Congress. Several weeks before Election Day, the House passed the Ratepayer Protection Act by a 417-3 vote. The bill would require states to consider adopting a policy that data centers pay for the upgrades necessary to meet their high electricity needs. The three nay House votes were from progressives who felt the bill’s measures, which would be voluntary, didn’t go far enough to protect consumers.

Similar concerns killed the Senate version, a reminder that even allies sometimes follow different strategic paths. Some proponents of tighter regulation will accept incremental progress, while others push for more sweeping change.
Brookings Institution scholars anticipate that the newly elected Congress will take up the issue again, this time with a directive to states to establish mandatory, not voluntary, requirements.

As the midterm elections approached, candidates up and down the ballot blanketed the airwaves and digital platforms with ads against data centers. President Donald Trump pushed back, suggesting that data center opponents want their communities to be “backwards and poor.”
Some Republican candidates walked a fine line between responding to voters’ concerns and not alienating the president.

It matters little whether the data center electoral narrative is accurate, and so far, the reported evidence is limited. We need to know where losing candidates stood on data centers, not just the winners. That voters considered data centers important says nothing about which direction they leaned. And despite a 98% success rate across the 41 local ballot measures, it’s hard to gauge how much resistance there is to the more than 600 proposed data centers that are slated to be built.

What does matter is that many people apparently are accepting the narrative because that alone will affect politics and the economy. Consider Elon Musk’s post on Nov. 4 on X, his social media platform: “Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now,” and the sell-off of data center-related stocks the next day.

As the 2028 presidential primaries come into focus, I believe we should expect to see many Democratic and Republican hopefuls emphasizing their support for data center restrictions and bans as they throw their hats into the ring.

articles.title: Young Black men in Philly are more likely to be pulled over if driving with friends, study shows
articles.author: Lance Hannon, Professor of Sociology and Criminology, Villanova University
paras: Deciding whether to drive somewhere alone or with friends is typically a matter of convenience or personal preference. But for young Black men in Philadelphia, that decision may carry an additional consideration: the likelihood of being pulled over by police.
My recent co-authored research suggests that young Black men traveling together attract significantly more police scrutiny than those driving alone.
In fact, the apparent effect of traveling with another young Black man was larger than the racial disparity detected when comparing young Black and white male drivers.
These findings challenge a common assumption about racial profiling: that its defining feature is simply whether a driver is Black or white.
What 41,633 traffic stops reveal

As a criminologist, I have published numerous peer-reviewed articles on police stops. I recently published a study on this topic in the journal Race and Social Problems with Molly Biddle, who at the time of writing was a data analyst for the Police Accountability Unit at the Defender Association of Philadelphia. In that study, we analyzed Philadelphia Police Department traffic stop records from 2021 through 2024.

We focused on men ages 18-29 stopped for motor vehicle code violations that did not involve an arrest. Among young Black males, approximately 1 in 4 were investigated alongside another young Black man in the car. Among young white males, less than 1 in 20 were investigated with another young white man.
This fivefold disparity is striking, but it does not necessarily establish discriminatory policing. Different groups might have different driving habits or preferences for traveling together.
To investigate whether police decisions contributed to this disparity, we employed a statistical technique known as the “veil-of-darkness” test.
What changes when the Sun goes down?
The veil-of-darkness test takes advantage of the fact that sunset occurs at different times throughout the year.

For example, an officer may be able to clearly see a vehicle’s occupants from a distance at 7 p.m. during summer but have a much more obscured view at the same hour during winter. Importantly, the idea is that daylight visibility can help an officer distinguish who is in the vehicle before the decision is made to pull the car over.

By comparing stops occurring at similar times under different lighting conditions, researchers can investigate whether the ability to distinguish vehicle occupants from afar influences traffic enforcement.
Our results revealed two important patterns.

First, the disparity between young Black men stopped and young white men stopped decreased when it was harder to see who is in the car. This is consistent with what other researchers have found using earlier data for Philadelphia.
Second, and this is what makes our analysis novel, we found that obscured visibility had an even greater impact on reducing the gap between young Black males stopped in groups versus driving alone.
Both patterns were statistically significant, even after accounting for time of day, neighborhood, police assignment, season and other factors.
These findings suggest that the visibility of a young Black male passenger in a vehicle may influence police decisions as much or even more than the visibility of a driver’s race alone.

Social psychological research offers a possible explanation for our results. People sometimes perceive groups as more threatening than individuals, and racial stereotypes can intensify those perceptions.
Two young Black men together may therefore be perceived as much more suspicious than either would be individually.

Indeed, in our sample, young Black male drivers investigated with young Black male passengers were far more likely to be pulled out of the vehicle and fruitlessly frisked for contraband than to receive a citation for the traffic offense used to justify the encounter in the first place. Only 7% were ticketed, which suggests that many stops were pretextual.
Racial profiling isn’t just about the driver’s race
Our recent findings build on our earlier study that examined more than 76,000 traffic stops involving Black drivers in predominantly Black Philadelphia neighborhoods.

That research found that the proportional representation of younger Black men among stopped drivers increased with daylight visibility, while the proportional representation of older Black women decreased.
The estimated magnitude of this within-race disparity was comparable to estimates commonly reported in studies comparing stops of Black versus white motorists.

Together, our two studies reveal that unfair differences in police scrutiny within the Black population can be as large as, or larger than, disparities detected through conventional Black-white comparisons.

Beyond investigating the extent to which the police pull over a greater quantity of Black drivers than white drivers, our research points to the need for police accountability advocates to ask additional questions about passengers and intraracial disparities.

For example, when policing in virtually all-Black communities, are some officers more blind to a driver’s age and gender than others? Likewise, are certain officers more likely to pull over young Black men when they are seen traveling in groups?
Such questions call attention to the idea that fairness within communities is just as important as fairness between them.

articles.title: A thank-you on Veterans Day won’t close the growing military-civilian gap
articles.author: Scott Parrott, Professor of Media Effects, School of Journalism and Mass Communications, University of South Carolina
paras: When the voice came over the plane’s PA system, it seemed familiar yet surprising: “Hello, everybody.”

“What?!” a passenger shouted, shocked. Others laughed and rose from their seats as former President Barack Obama appeared in person and welcomed the airplane of veterans to Washington before Veterans Day in 2025. They had flown from Wisconsin to Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport aboard an Honor Flight to see the capital’s monuments to military service.

“I wanted to stop by and just say thank you for your extraordinary service – to you, your family,” Obama said in brief remarks later posted to social media. “The sacrifices that all of you made to protect our country is something that will always be honored.”

Obama’s post was one of 399,000 references to veterans on the social media platform X on Veterans Day last year, Nov. 11, 2025. The annual holiday was established to “solemnly remember the sacrifices of all those who fought so valiantly on the seas, in the air and on foreign shores, to preserve our heritage of freedom,” as President Dwight D. Eisenhower proclaimed.

The hundreds of thousands of posts are compelling to me as a social scientist who studies how veterans are represented in the media. The volume of commentary illustrates Americans’ desire to recognize veterans, but it also captures the transience of public attention.
By the following Tuesday, Nov. 18, 2025, the number of references to veterans plummeted by 374,000, or nearly 94%. The news cycle had moved on.

The shift was not particularly surprising. My research shows that social media mentions of veterans peak in positive sentiment at two points each year: Veterans Day and Memorial Day. The rest of the time, the conversations on social media are largely driven by news outlets releasing stories and politicians announcing programs and events.

Indeed, social and other mass media play a role in what experts describe as a military-civilian gap. Put simply, while U.S. adults hold the military in high regard, they do not understand the institution or the experiences of its personnel despite its importance in domestic and international affairs and its US$900 billion in taxpayer funding.
This military-civilian gap can create problems when it comes to military recruitment, civilians’ ability to identify with neighbors who serve and veterans reintegrating into civilian society.

The military-civilian gap exists in part because, since the draft ended in 1973, the share of Americans who have served in the armed forces has declined. Only about 6% of adults were veterans in 2022, a decline from 18% in 1980. Compounding the issue, a decreasing proportion of U.S. adults personally know someone who has served. That means much of the population is learning about military life through mass media representation.

Journalists gravitate toward stories in which the subject matter is timely, emotional or full of conflict, because these qualities engage audiences. They operate on tight deadlines with limited resources. They also face restricted access to the Pentagon.

That means news outlets may be more inclined to cover a holiday, charity event or violent crime involving veterans than to take deep dives into the military budget or examine the role of veteran-owned businesses in the local economy.
Because of this, veterans end up typecast as heroes or victims of their service.
Politicians also influence which issues people in the U.S. see in the news or discuss on social media, but the share of members of Congress with military experience has plummeted since the 1970s.

In a 2018 study, our research team examined how news organizations in all 50 states represented veterans in news stories shared on X. In analyzing 1,460 stories, we identified three themes, which together described a majority of stories: veterans as heroes, as recipients of charity, or as victims of mental or physical harm.

Some military veterans may be heroes, and some may face challenges related to trauma, reintegrating into civilian society or navigating government bureaucracy. Such coverage may certainly be newsworthy.

The problem, according to critics of veterans’ representation in news media, is that not much else appears in the media. As one veteran told a researcher, “It doesn’t sell newspapers that Joe Smith from Davenport went to Afghanistan three times, got out of the military, went to college, and now works as an account manager for American Eagle.”

But media representations of social groups shape our perceptions of the world. A 2021 experiment found that exposure to stereotypical news stories about veterans led readers to associate veterans with post-traumatic stress disorder, a misunderstood and stigmatized condition. This, in turn, led readers to feel less desire to be socially close with veterans. The outcome illustrated how stories can have unintended downstream consequences even when journalists are covering newsworthy topics – in this case, PTSD and homelessness.

We also tested whether reading a second story – one in which veterans talked about media stereotypes – would dampen those negative effects. It worked, illustrating the importance of a news feed that provides nuance.

In another study, we asked 1,047 U.S. adults to picture a veteran, describe the veteran and then explain where the image originated. When people depended on media for their image, rather than personal experience, they called to mind stereotypical images such as homelessness, PTSD and heroism.

Given these stereotypes, a number of veterans organizations are advocating for broader, more insightful media representation. Military Veterans in Journalism and Veterans in Media & Entertainment are nonprofits that help veterans pursue professional careers in news and entertainment media, motivated in part by the potential for veterans to produce nuanced stories about military life. There are also nonprofit news organizations, such as The War Horse, seeking to bridge the military-civilian gap through storytelling and investigative reporting.

Media can draw attention to veterans. Obama’s airport surprise racked up 10.8 million views, 136,000 likes and 18,000 shares on X. But it will take more than made-for-media moments to bridge the military-civilian gap. That includes taking conversations with veterans offline.

In a 2019 study, U.S. Air Force Maj. Nicholas J. Mercurio conducted focus groups with veterans and active-duty service members and asked how they felt about “reflexive and formulaic expressions of gratitude” from the public such as “thank you for your service.”

Responses were mixed, in part because veterans assumed civilians did not understand what that service entailed. Nonetheless, there was general agreement that civilians could go beyond thank you by showing interest in the personal experiences of veterans and having sincere conversations about their jobs.
In doing so, civilians can demonstrate “interest in the individual,” Mercurio wrote, “not what they represent.”

articles.title: The surprising origins of Denmark’s reputation for open-mindedness
articles.author: Detlef Siegfried, Professor of Modern German and European History, University of Copenhagen
paras: Ask Danes what makes Denmark Danish and you might hear about openness, tolerance and the freedom to live as you choose.

You can see it in the country’s history: Denmark was the first country in the world to legalise pornography. Alternative communities such as Christiania in Copenhagen are internationally famous for their counterculture and liberal attitudes. And Danish activists have helped push ideas about sexuality and family life in new directions.
But there is a less obvious part of this story.
Denmark did not develop its reputation for open-mindedness entirely on its own. Some of the people who helped create that image were looking at Denmark from across the border.

From the 1960s onwards, West Germany became an important audience for Denmark’s emerging reputation as a more liberal society. For young Germans frustrated with what they saw as a conservative, hierarchical and authoritarian society, Denmark looked like a place where people had more freedom to experiment with different ways of living.

West Germany in the 1960s and 1970s was still grappling with the legacy of Nazism. Many young people in the West German New Left rejected the social and political values of their parents’ generation and looked for alternatives.
The situation was also different across the German divide. In East Germany, the communist state offered its own very different model of society and controlled many aspects of public and private life.
For young West Germans seeking alternatives, Denmark seemed like something else entirely: a nearby democratic country where social experimentation seemed possible.

Research I am carrying out with my colleague Tobias Haimin de Fønss Wung-Sung into West German reactions to Denmark during this period shows how several aspects of Danish life contributed to this image.

Christiania, the self-governing community in Copenhagen, became associated with communal living and alternative lifestyles. The New Left political movement challenged established politics and social norms. Roskilde music festival grew into an important gathering place for young people and counterculture. Denmark also experimented with progressive approaches to education and pornography.
From abroad, this created an image of Denmark as a country where people were unusually free to live differently.

In 1969, when the Danish parliament legalised pornographic images , its decision was highly controversial among Danes. But it attracted considerable attention internationally, particularly in West Germany, where the new government under Chancellor Willy Brandt prepared a similar reform.
The result was not simply a change in Danish law. People, products and money began moving across the border.

Government officials travelled to Copenhagen to learn about the effects of the liberalisation. West Germans travelled to Denmark to buy pornography. Danish producers gained access to a much larger market south of the border. Denmark could even be imagined in West Germany as a kind of porn paradise.
Our research into West German reactions to Denmark’s liberalisation between 1965 and 1985 shows how the country became associated with a new kind of sexual freedom.

Danish homosexual people and activists also developed connections with larger gay communities in West Germany, particularly in Berlin and Hamburg. And Denmark developed its own naturist culture, not least inspired by the German movement of freikörperkultur (pronounced FRY-kur-per-kul-toor) or “free body culture”. People gathered to swim, sunbathe and socialise naked.
People, ideas and practices were therefore moving in both directions across the border.
Reputation and national values
Over time, these developments helped turn Denmark’s reputation for social liberalism into something more than an international image. It became part of how Denmark could describe itself.

In 2016, for example, the Danish government asked the public to identify values considered particularly important to Danish society. The resulting Danmarkskanon, or Danish Canon, included ten such values. One was frisind (pronounced free-sin) – a word that can mean open-mindedness, tolerance or freedom from conventional moral constraints.

The Canon described frisind in terms of openness towards traditional moral ideas, the body and sexuality. It pointed to Denmark’s relaxed attitude towards nudity, tolerance of different forms of family and sexual life, alternative lifestyles and the legalisation of pornography.

By this point, what had once been a contested and internationally shaped reputation had become something that could be presented as part of Denmark’s cultural heritage. But that does not necessarily mean Danes have always been uniquely tolerant.

The Danish criminologist Berl Kutchinsky (1935-1995) studied the liberalisation of pornography extensively and he was sceptical of precisely this idea. He argued that Denmark’s exceptional liberalism was something of a myth.

In his view, Danes still belonged to the broadly “puritanical, post-Victorian” family of European nations. Denmark was simply among the less puritanical members of that group, alongside Sweden, the Netherlands and Germany. Compared with them, he considered Danes “slightly more liberal and permissive” when it came to sexuality.
If Kutchinsky was right, Danish frisind is less about being uniquely liberal than about being liberal in comparison with particular neighbours.
The history of Danish frisind therefore stretches well beyond Denmark.

And while it has been shaped by changing laws and attitudes inside the country, people travelling across the border, activists building international networks and products finding new markets have also played a role.
That is easy to lose sight of once an idea becomes part of a national identity.

The Danish Canon presents frisind as a Danish value. But its history suggests something more complicated: Denmark’s reputation for open-mindedness was, at least partly, made through its relationships with other countries.
In other words, one of the very things Denmark considers particularly Danish likely started out more as a comparison with somewhere else.

articles.title: Georgia Gov.-elect Keisha Lance Bottoms stands on the shoulders of Stacey Abrams, Charlotta Bass and countless other Black women who dreamed
articles.author: Allissa V. Richardson, Associate Professor of Journalism, USC Annenberg School for Communication and Journalism
paras: There are elections that change the political map. And then there are elections that make you wonder whether the land itself remembers.
The auction blocks. The cotton fields. The lynching trees. The Black women who cleaned governors’ homes but could not dream of becoming governor themselves.
And now Keisha Lance Bottoms has been elected Georgia’s first Black woman governor. The first Black woman elected governor of any American state.
Bottoms has traced her ancestry back five generations to an enslaved person on a plantation near Crawfordville, Georgia.
An ancestor held in bondage on Georgia soil. A descendant elected to govern it.
The same earth. An entirely different claim to power. How many women had to believe in a future they would never live to see?

Bottoms’s victory represents the paradox of Black political advancement amid racial violence and the often-unrecognized labor of women who build futures they may never inhabit. Ultimately, Bottoms’ victory reflects both extraordinary progress and the unfinished work of American democracy.
The children who deserved a future
I keep thinking about the little children.

Between 1979 and 1981, Atlanta was terrorized by the disappearances and murders of Black children and young adults. Mothers pleaded for answers. Families lived in a city where childhood itself had become dangerous.

The murders unfolded just years after Maynard Jackson’s historic 1973 election as Atlanta’s first Black mayor. His victory announced a new era of Black political power. Yet that power could not shield the city’s most vulnerable children. Suspicions of Ku Klux Klan involvement circulated, although the Klan’s responsibility was never established.
That distinction matters. So does the fear.

Bottoms was born in 1970. She was 9 when the murders began. She grew up in the same Atlanta where Black parents searched desperately for their missing children. She belonged to the generation whose futures were being stolen. And now she is preparing to lead the entire state.
What a terrible, beautiful, complicated thing.
Those murdered children were not symbols waiting to become useful to history. They were sons and daughters who deserved the ordinary miracle of growing older. They deserved a future.

Bottoms later occupied the mayor’s office that Jackson first opened to Black leadership. Now she is preparing to occupy the governor’s mansion. History has not erased its cruelty. But it has delivered an astonishing answer.
And this victory does not belong to Bottoms alone.
The woman who sowed the seeds
This victory belongs, in no small measure, to democracy advocate, legislator and lawyer Stacey Abrams. Perhaps those who recognize what Abrams made possible have sent her flowers.

Abrams ran for Georgia governor in 2018 and 2022. She lost both races. But through the New Georgia Project and Fair Fight, organizations focused on engaging voters and protecting voting rights, she helped build an electorate that could imagine Georgia differently. She registered voters, challenged barriers to participation, and refused to accept that the South’s political future was fixed.

And now another Black woman has won the office Abrams twice sought, in the third gubernatorial race in a row headed by a Black Democratic woman. There is something biblical about the path Abrams steadfastly cleared. I think of Moses, guiding his people toward the Promised Land but never entering it himself.

Abrams’ journey is not over. Nor should her accomplishments be measured by another woman’s victory. But I believe there is sacred work in preparing a future you may never personally enjoy. Some people plant trees. Some people sit in their shade. Stacey Abrams planted. Bottoms is standing beneath the branches.
And as a scholar of Black media history, I can reach even further back, to another woman who understood the audacity of claiming political power: Charlotta Bass.
In 1952, Bass became the first Black woman nominated for vice president of the United States, running on the Progressive Party ticket.
The future Charlotta dared to imagine
Before the Voting Rights Act in 1965, before the March on Washington in 1963, before Jackson was elected mayor in 1973 and before Abrams or Bottoms drew their first breaths, there was Bass.

A Black newspaper publisher who confronted segregation, police brutality and white supremacist violence in her four-decade ownership of The California Eagle, Bass understood that political power was about more than winning office. It was about who had the right to imagine themselves in one.

Bass ran when a Black woman entering the White House seemed almost unimaginable. Almost. But not to her. I imagine she would have loved this election. And I suspect she would have had pointed questions for Gov.-elect Bottoms.
What will you do for the poor? The disenfranchised? How will you protect the vote that brought you here?

History-making is not the same as justice-making, and representation matters. The true measure of Bottoms’ victory will be whether Georgians experience the more just state she promised to bring about.

For generations, Black women have been asked to save a democracy that would not save them. We have carried clipboards, protest signs and entire movements on our backs. We have been told to wait. To be patient. To be grateful.
And now a Black woman has been elected to govern Georgia.

The children have not returned. The past has not been undone. But something has shifted. Charlotta dreamed it. Stacey helped build it. Keisha has won it. And somewhere, another little Black girl is watching. She may not understand the history. She may only know that the governor-elect looks like her. For now, that is enough to begin a dream.
And history has taught us what can happen when a Black girl begins to dream.

articles.title: Labour’s immigration dilemma: with social care exceptions, the party is trying to have it both ways
articles.author: Erica Consterdine, Senior Lecturer in Public Policy, Lancaster University
paras: Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood’s headline announcement on immigration centred on how long someone must spend in the UK before they can be granted indefinite leave to remain (ILR). She said this period will double from five to ten years – but social care workers will be exempt. This proposal was widely expected, but exempting social care workers is a U-turn for the government.

The proposals were met with a mixed response. Some on the left said the qualifying period is too high, while others on the right claimed the plans were too lax on immigration by exempting care workers.

Many migrants came to the UK on the understanding that five years of lawful residence would provide a path to settlement. So the government’s decision to retrospectively change those terms raises serious questions about fairness, trust and the legitimacy of immigration policy.

The UK is now moving towards one of the toughest settlement and naturalisation systems in Europe. In fact, this direction is more readily associated with the political right than a Labour government that presents itself as committed to equality, workers’ rights and social justice. So where are we now with immigration policy, and what does this shift tell us about British politics?

The tough naturalisation requirements come off the back of 16 years of restrictive rhetoric on immigration across the political spectrum. From 2010, the Conservative-led coalition government set a pledge to reduce net migration from hundreds of thousands to the tens of thousands. And since then, successive administrations and opposition parties have attempted to outflank each other on tough immigration talk.

The last Conservative government lurched towards nativist, exclusionary rhetoric, and draconian policy proposals in a bid to outmanoeuvre Reform UK. The result has been to keep immigration high on the public agenda (though with ebbs and flows following Brexit and COVID).

Yet despite the tough talk, the combination of an economy that needs migrant labour as well as humanitarian schemes for citizens of Hong Kong and Ukraine, took net migration to the highest level on record. This was in 2023, the year before the Conservatives left office.

Critically, while previous governments talked tough on immigration, Brexit left major shortages in the labour market, especially in some of the low-paid jobs that many Britons do not want to do. As a result, a number of policy schemes were introduced to plug these gaps, including the health and care visa.

This scheme proved popular, resulting in 106,000 visas being issued to social care workers (the figure excludes their dependants) in 2023. But since then, more scrutiny on sponsors and the decision to stop dependants coming to the UK on this visa have led to sharp declines.

Labour has long been dogged on immigration. The party spent most of its years in opposition apologising for apparent mistakes made in office over the managed migration programme. This was a series of policies that resulted in one of the most expansive immigration policies in Europe.

And ideologically, immigration has always been a headache for Labour. Like other social democratic parties, Labour is torn between its protectionist trade union roots, which favour tighter borders, and its rights-based tradition of protecting migrants.

The dilemma is further complicated by Labour’s neoliberal turn since the Blair era, which saw globalisation as inevitable and embraced flexible labour migration as a way of controlling inflation. In short, Labour has been complicit in deepening a labour market that depends on on migration for its workforce, while using the “secure borders” rhetoric.

These ideological tensions are reflected in the make-up of both the Labour party and its electorate, bringing together members and constituents with competing values and priorities – the “beer drinkers” and the “wine drinkers”. And they are precisely why the new rules contain a mixed bag of restrictions and concessions on social-care visas.

Andy Burnham’s government has faced this tension head on, with many in the party lambasting Mahmood’s pursuit of high thresholds for naturalisation. Prominent figures including Housing Secretary Angela Rayner had accused Mahmood of “pulling the rug” from underneath people. This intra-party tension resulted in the decision to exempt social care workers.

Policies that increase immigration are never generally vote winners. But social democratic parties have a choice whether to keep quiet on the issue, accommodate pressures from the right, or attempt to walk a middle ground of selective immigration.

Former prime minister Keir Starmer was accused of echoing right-wing rhetoric and produced the restrictive white paper from which the new policies stem. In practice, Labour’s approach is built on contribution-based residency – the more you earn the longer you can stay.

So far, Burnham has largely sailed the same ship, maintaining Mahommod as home secretary and changing little of the direction on immigration. Yet his recent comments on humanitarian schemes and reopening the debate on free movement suggest that the tide might be beginning to turn. Mahmood’s U-turn on social care workers might be part of this shift.

articles.title: What Tommy Robinson’s conviction tells us about the cost to journalists reporting in the public interest
articles.author: Tom Felle, Associate Professor of Journalism, University of Galway
paras: During the unrest that followed the 2024 Southport murders, British tabloid the Daily Mail reported on the activities of far-right activist Tommy Robinson. The story was covered by freelance reporter Andrew Young, and edited by the Mail’s own Jacob Dirnhuber.

On October 28, Robinson was convicted for threatening and harassing Young and Dirnhuber. A jury at Southwark Crown Court in London found Robinson guilty of two counts of harassment causing fear of violence, an offence with a maximum sentence of ten years. The judge will sentence him on December 16.

Robinson, whose real name is Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, hired private investigators to find the journalists’ home addresses. He messaged Dirnhuber saying “I’ll be knocking at your door”, and told Young by phone “I’m coming to get you”. He also posted images of Dirnhuber outside his home, and of Young’s family.
Before Robinson’s conviction, Young was given a close protection officer, while Dirnhuber was forced to move house.

Anyone is entitled to criticise the Daily Mail or challenge its reporting. In a democratic society, any member of the public must be free to challenge what journalists publish. But journalists must also be free to report without fearing threats of violence, whether online or in their homes.

In reality, threats to reporters’ homes and families, along with online abuse and physical intimidation, have become so pervasive that they are treated as part of the job in Britain and well beyond it.

Few of these cases end up in front of a jury, yet Robinson’s conviction shows that the law can respond. Prosecutors told an earlier hearing that none of the alleged harassment contained a direct threat of violence, and the jury still convicted.

Robinson’s victims had a national newspaper behind them, but many journalists have no such support. When threats make journalists or their editors think twice about a story, the public loses out, usually without ever knowing.

The Robinson case is one among many, and around the world journalists are increasingly under threat for doing their jobs. The Committee to Protect Journalists found a record 129 journalists and media workers were killed in 2025, more than three-quarters of them in conflict settings.
Europe is not immune: hired killers murdered Daphne Caruana Galizia in Malta in 2017, and Ján Kuciak in Slovakia in 2018, both investigative journalists.

Most threats never come near that point, but they are very common. In a 2020 global survey by UNESCO and the International Center for Journalists, 73% of the women journalists who responded had experienced online attacks, and one in five reported being attacked or abused offline in connection with it.

In research commissioned by the UK government and published in July this year, 72% of the 531 journalists surveyed had experienced harassment, abuse, threats or legal intimidation. Among those affected, almost half said safety concerns had made them hesitate before reporting certain stories.
These figures should concern anyone who relies on journalists to uncover what those in power would prefer to keep quiet.

Online abuse is far more pervasive than physical violence, and it takes a heavy toll. Among those affected in the aforementioned UK government survey, 78% had faced online abuse, compared with 11% who had been physically attacked. Just over half said safety concerns had damaged their wellbeing, and almost one in four had considered leaving journalism.

Female journalists are at an increased risk of being targeted. In a 2026 UN Women study, nearly a quarter of female journalists and media workers surveyed had been diagnosed with or treated for anxiety or depression linked to online violence. Some 45% said they self-censored on social media to avoid abuse – a 50% increase on 2020 – and more than one in five self-censored in their day-to-day work.
My own research on abuse of women in Irish politics raises a related question about who can afford to stay visible in public life when doing so exposes them to threats.

Reporting the abuse often brings little relief. Only 17% of affected journalists in the UK government survey had gone to the police, and a little over one in four of those found it effective. Of those who reported to online platforms, just 5% found that route effective.

The Daily Mail deserves credit for standing by its journalists, but not every news organisation can afford to do the same, and many freelancers have no one to call. If reporters fear for their safety because of online or offline threats, stories will go untold, and those in power will face fewer questions. Democracy will suffer as a result, and we all lose out.
